nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'cell phone', 'cell', or 'phone' in conversation, and 'smartphone' for modern models with apps. 'Mobile phone' is more common in British English. Writers in the US also use 'cellphone' as a one-word spelling.

distinctions.note: The two mean the same thing; 'cell phone' is the standard two-word form, while 'cellphone' appears more often in informal or tech writing.
A smartphone is a cell phone with apps and internet access; not every cell phone is a smartphone.

examples.everyday: Sorry I missed your call; my cell phone was on silent.
examples.professional: Could you send me your cell phone number so I can reach you if the meeting runs late?
examples.analytical: The spread of the cell phone changed how people coordinate, turning ordinary time into always-reachable time.

nuance.analogy: A cell phone is a radio that hops from tower to tower as you drive.
nuance.etymology: 'Cell' comes from Latin cella, 'small room,' and refers to the coverage areas, or cells, that each tower serves.
common_mistakes: Saying 'mobile phone' in American conversation; Americans usually say 'cell phone'.
Stressing PHONE strongly, as in 'cell-PHONE'; the stress normally falls on CELL.

conversation.text: Please turn off your cell phone before the service begins.
What's your cell phone number in case I get lost?
I left my cell phone in the car.

senses.definition: An enclosed space, usually fully underground (in some cases partly underground), often under a building, used for storage or shelter.
senses.example: The farmhouse has several additions, added over many decades; it has three cellars, and one of them is older than the other two.

senses.definition: A wine collection, especially when stored in a cellar.
senses.example: The insurance company valued his cellar at $27,000, largely on the strength of his bottles of 1972 Château Hypothetica.

senses.definition: Last place in a league or competition; some rank near last place.
senses.example: The Tigers have been in the cellar all year long, and I'm tired of it.

senses.definition: A basement.
senses.example: Most of my tools and hardware are in the garage, but I keep some tools in the cellar, too, mainly for convenience.

senses.definition: Salt cellar.
To store (something, especially food or wine) in a cellar.

core.definition: An underground or partly underground room, often under a house, used for storing food, wine, or other goods.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The second syllable is a weak, reduced vowel, so say it as 'er' with the r pronounced, not as a full 'ell-ah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a physical place and carries no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'basement' for the underground floor of a house where people live or keep things, and 'cellar' more often for a small, cool storage room for wine, potatoes, or canned food, or for an older underground room. Sports writers also use 'cellar' for the bottom of a standings table, as in 'the team finished in the cellar.'

distinctions.note: A basement is the finished or unfinished lower floor of a house, often used for living space. A cellar is usually smaller, used mainly for storage, and may be older or more fully underground.
A storeroom is any room for keeping supplies and does not need to be underground. A cellar is specifically below ground level.

examples.everyday: We keep the potatoes in the cellar, where it stays cool all summer.
examples.professional: Our data center sits in a cellar room, so we had to check the flood risk before we moved the servers.
examples.analytical: The cellar, as a space set apart from the living rooms above, becomes in the parable a symbol of hidden storage and concealed provision.

nuance.analogy: A cellar is like a hidden pantry under the house: a cool, dark place where things are saved for later.
nuance.etymology: From Latin cellarium, 'storeroom for provisions,' from cella, 'small room.'
common_mistakes: Using 'cellar' for any basement with living space, when Americans usually say 'basement' for that.
Saying 'the cellar of the house' when 'the cellar under the house' or 'in the cellar' is more natural.

cellar.etymology: From Middle English *celer*, *seler*, from Anglo-Norman *celer*, Old French *celier* (modern *cellier*), from Late Latin *cellārium*, from Latin *cella*.

senses.definition: The act of chastising; rebuke; punishment.

core.definition: Harsh criticism or punishment given to correct someone's behavior.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is pronounced 'tiz' as in 'is', not 'tize' as in 'eyes', so the word has three clear syllables.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies a painful correction, often from someone in authority, though in religious usage it can be understood as loving discipline.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use chastisement in everyday speech; it sounds formal, religious or literary. You may hear it in sermons, in discussions of parenting, or in news about an official's rebuke. In casual talk say 'a scolding', 'a talking-to' or 'getting in trouble'. A natural reply to 'That was a harsh chastisement' is 'Yeah, he was really hard on them.'

distinctions.note: Punishment is a general word for a penalty; chastisement is more personal and focuses on correction, often through words or rebuke.
Scolding is an everyday word for telling someone off; chastisement is more formal and can imply something more serious.

examples.everyday: Her mom's chastisement was short, but he got the message and cleaned his room.
examples.professional: Public chastisement in a team chat rarely fixes the problem and usually makes people stop raising concerns.
examples.analytical: Hebrews 12 presents chastisement as a sign of God's fatherly care, which changes how discipline itself is understood.

nuance.etymology: From chastise plus the suffix -ment, denoting the act or result of chastising.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in chas-TIZ-ment; the stress belongs on the first syllable.
Using chastisement for everyday criticism; it sounds heavy and formal, so 'criticism' or 'scolding' is usually better.

chastisement.etymology: From Old French *chastiement*, from the verb *chastier*, from Latin *castīgō*.

senses.definition: Belief in an earthly thousand-year period of peace and prosperity, sometimes equated with the return of Jesus for that period.

core.definition: The belief that Christ will reign on earth for a thousand years of peace before the end of history.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and 'ch' is a hard 'k' as in Greek words. The ending -asm is a reduced 'az-um'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in scholarship; historically it was sometimes used as a pejorative label by opponents.
nuance.usage_note: Used mostly by theologians and church historians as a Greek-derived synonym for premillennialism. Ordinary Americans say 'millennialism' or 'premillennialism'. Early church writers such as Papias and Irenaeus are often called chiliasts.

distinctions.note: Millennialism is the broader and more common term; chiliasm is the older Greek-derived word.
Premillennialism says Christ returns before the thousand years; chiliasm stresses the literal thousand-year earthly reign.
Amillennialism reads the thousand years symbolically and rejects a literal earthly reign.

examples.everyday: My professor said the word for believing in a literal thousand-year reign is chiliasm.
examples.professional: In today's seminar we'll trace chiliasm from Papias through Irenaeus to Augustine's reaction.
examples.analytical: Augustine's reading of Revelation 20 as the present age effectively displaced the chiliasm of the earlier fathers.

nuance.etymology: From Greek chilias, 'a thousand', from chilioi, 'thousand'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'ch' as in 'church' instead of 'k'.
Stressing the second syllable.
Treating it as identical to all forms of millennialism.
nuance.biblical_note: The idea rests on Revelation 20:1-6, which describes a thousand-year reign of Christ with the saints after Satan is bound. The Greek word chilia ete means 'a thousand years'. Interpreters differ on whether the period is literal or symbolic.

senses.definition: Synonym of millenarian: a person who believes the Second Coming of Jesus Christ will involve his physical rule on Earth for 1000 years.

core.definition: A person who believes Jesus will return to rule the earth for a literal thousand years of peace before the final judgment.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on KIL. The ch is a k sound, the middle syllable is short, and the final -ast rhymes with fast, not with -est.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in scholarly writing, though some critics use it to suggest naive or fanatical expectations.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use chiliast mainly in theological and church history writing. In ordinary church conversation, people usually say millennialist or premillennialist. Use the word precisely, and remember that some believers would reject the label.

distinctions.note: Millenarian is broader and can describe religious or secular believers in a coming golden age, while chiliast refers specifically to Christian believers in a literal thousand-year reign.
Premillennialist is a specific modern term for those who believe Christ returns before the millennium, while chiliast is a more historical term.
Amillennialist describes someone who reads the thousand years symbolically, so it contrasts directly with a chiliast's literal reading.

examples.everyday: My uncle calls himself a chiliast, so he's always talking about the end times over dinner.
examples.professional: Our seminary reading list includes three chiliasts, so the course will compare their readings of Revelation 20.
examples.analytical: Papias and Justin are often cited as chiliasts, though modern scholars debate how literally they read the thousand years.

nuance.analogy: Like someone with a calendar marked for the day everything is finally set right on earth.
nuance.etymology: From chiliasm, from Greek chilias ('thousand') with the agent suffix -ist.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with chiliad, a word for a group of one thousand.
Using chiliast as a general word for any optimist; it refers specifically to belief in a literal thousand-year reign.
Pronouncing the first syllable with a long i or a ch sound as in chill.

chiliast.etymology: From Latin *chiliasta*, possibly via French *chiliaste*, from Ancient Greek *χιλιαστής*, from *χῑ́λιοι* (“thousand”) + *-αστής* (“-ast, -ist: forming agent nouns”).

senses.definition: A small evergreen tree native to Sri Lanka and southern India, Cinnamomum verum or Cinnamomum zeylanicum, belonging to the family Lauraceae.
Several related trees, notably the Indonesian cinnamon (Cinnamomum burmanni) and Chinese cinnamon or cassia (Cinnamomum aromaticum or Cinnamomum cassia).
A spice from the dried aromatic bark of the cinnamon tree, either rolled into strips or ground into a powder. The word is commonly used as a trade name for spices made of any of the species above.
senses.example: cinnamon toast

senses.definition: True cinnamon, the product made of Cinnamomum verum.
A warm yellowish-brown color, the color of cinnamon.
senses.example: cinnamon:

senses.definition: Containing cinnamon, or having a cinnamon taste.
Of a yellowish-brown color.

core.definition: A reddish-brown spice made from the dried inner bark of a tropical tree, used in baking, drinks and desserts.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the middle and last syllables to a quick, neutral 'uh'. Non-native speakers often give every syllable equal weight or say 'sin-a-MON'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests warmth, baking, holidays and comfort food.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cinnamon constantly for sweet foods like cinnamon rolls, apple pie and French toast, and in coffee or oatmeal. Ground cinnamon sold in a jar is the everyday form; cinnamon sticks are used for drinks and slow cooking. When ordering, you can say 'with cinnamon' or 'cinnamon sugar' without any special phrasing.

distinctions.note: Cassia is a related, coarser and stronger bark from a different tree species, often sold as cinnamon in US grocery stores; true cinnamon is milder and more delicate.
Nutmeg is the seed of a different tropical tree, with a warmer, nuttier flavor, though both are used in the same baked goods.

examples.everyday: Can you grab the cinnamon from the cabinet? I want to sprinkle some on the oatmeal.
examples.professional: The bakery team reformulated the cinnamon swirl recipe to cut the sugar by fifteen percent.
examples.analytical: The spice trade in antiquity made cinnamon a symbol of luxury, and its scarcity drove merchants to invent fanciful origin stories.

nuance.analogy: Cinnamon is like the warm, familiar background hum of a kitchen on a cold morning.
nuance.etymology: From Greek kinnamomon, probably borrowed from a Semitic language such as Hebrew qinnamon.
common_mistakes: Saying 'sin-a-MON' with stress on the last syllable.
Confusing the spice with cassia, which is a different and sharper product sold under the same name.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew qinnamon, a fragrant spice used in the holy anointing oil and incense of Israel. Exodus 30:23 lists it among the ingredients of the sacred anointing oil. Song of Songs 4:14 names it among the fragrant plants of the lover's garden. Revelation 18:13 lists it among the costly goods of Babylon's merchants, showing it as a symbol of luxury.

senses.definition: The act of coalescing.
The merging of two segments into one.

core.definition: The process of separate things coming together and joining into one whole, such as droplets merging or ideas forming a unified movement.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'les', and the final '-ence' is a reduced schwa plus 'ns', so it sounds like 'uns'. Do not pronounce the 'e' in '-ence' as a full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and precise. It has a scholarly tone and is rarely used in casual speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use coalescence mostly in science, physics, and academic writing, such as droplet coalescence or the coalescence of galaxies. In everyday conversation, people say 'coming together' or 'merging' instead. In professional settings, use it when you want to describe a clear, gradual unification of parts.

distinctions.note: A merger is a business or legal combination of organizations, while coalescence is a natural or gradual process of parts joining together.
Union emphasizes joining into a formal or organized whole, while coalescence stresses the gradual process of forming one mass or idea.

examples.everyday: The way the rain drops coalesce on the windshield is kind of satisfying to watch.
examples.professional: The data show rapid coalescence of user feedback into three recurring themes, which helped us prioritize the roadmap.
examples.analytical: Her account of the nation's coalescence depends on the assumption that shared grievances precede shared identity.

nuance.analogy: Like puddles on a driveway running together into one larger pool after a heavy rain.
nuance.etymology: From coalesce, from Latin coalescere, plus the noun suffix -ence.
common_mistakes: Confusing coalescence with cohesion, which describes the tendency of things to stick together rather than the process of merging.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying koh-uh-LES-ens with a full vowel in the last syllable.

coalescence.etymology: From Middle French *coalescence* and its etymon Latin *coalēscentia*.

senses.definition: A pricking of conscience or a feeling of regret, especially one which is slight or fleeting.

core.definition: A pang of conscience or guilt, or a feeling of moral hesitation about doing something wrong.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable: -PUNK-. The first syllable is a weak 'kum'. Say 'ng-k' together before 'shun'.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative feeling of guilt; but the quality is positive, as it shows a working conscience. Often seen in the negative phrase 'without compunction', which condemns coldness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'compunction' mainly in writing, and most often in negative form: 'He lied without compunction.' In spoken English, it can sound formal or ironic. In Orthodox spirituality, it names a deep, healthy sorrow for sin.

distinctions.note: Remorse is deeper regret after wrongdoing; compunction is often a slight prick before or after.
A scruple is a moral principle that holds you back; compunction is the feeling of guilt itself.
Guilt is the broad state of being at fault or feeling so; compunction is a milder, more fleeting pang.

examples.everyday: He ate the last slice of pizza without any compunction, even though it was mine.
examples.professional: The vendor raised prices without compunction, knowing we had no alternative before launch.
examples.analytical: In the Philokalia, compunction is not mere guilt but a grace that softens the heart and opens it to repentance.

nuance.analogy: Like a small pin pressing on your conscience.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin compunctio, from Latin compungere 'to prick sharply', from com- + pungere 'to prick'.
common_mistakes: Using it as a countable noun with 'a lot of compunctions' instead of 'much compunction'.
Using 'compunction for' instead of 'compunction about'.
Pronouncing it COM-punction.
nuance.biblical_note: The idea appears in Acts 2:37, where hearers were 'cut to the heart' by Peter's sermon, using Greek katanyssomai, 'to pierce'. Psalm 51 expresses a contrite heart. In Greek patristic and Orthodox writing, katanyxis ('piercing') names the sorrow that leads to repentance.

compunction.etymology: From Middle English *compunccion*, borrowed from Old French *compunction*, from Late Latin *compunctionem* (“a pricking”), from Latin *compunctus*, the past participle of *compungere* (“to severely prick”), from *com-* + *pungere* (“to prick”).

senses.definition: To puzzle, perplex, baffle, bewilder (somebody); to afflict by being complicated, contradictory, or otherwise difficult to understand.
senses.example: It confused me when I went to the office and nobody was there, but then I realized it was Sunday.

senses.definition: To mix up, muddle up (one thing with another); to mistake (one thing for another).
senses.example: People who say "hola" to Italians are confusing Italian with Spanish.

senses.definition: To mix thoroughly; to confound; to disorder.
senses.example: The dense fog utterly confused traffic on the highway.

senses.definition: To be confused.
(dated) To make uneasy and ashamed; to embarrass.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: Synonym of confused.

core.definition: To make someone unable to think clearly or understand something, or to mix up two things.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, FYOOZ. The first syllable is a reduced schwa, and the final s sounds like a z. Do not pronounce the first syllable as 'con' with a full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it describes a state of being unable to understand, which can be frustrating.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use confuse constantly in everyday speech, as in 'you're confusing me' or 'don't confuse the two.' Be careful not to say 'I'm confused me.' A common casual reply is 'Sorry, I didn't mean to confuse you,' which is polite and natural.

distinctions.note: Confound is more formal and literary, often suggesting utter bafflement; confuse is the everyday word.
Mix up is an informal phrasal verb for mistaking one thing for another; confuse can also mean mental puzzlement.

examples.everyday: Don't confuse the two brothers; one of them is the tall guy who works at the bakery.
examples.professional: The dashboard labels confuse users, so I suggest we rename the metrics before the launch.
examples.analytical: Paul warns the Corinthians that God is not a God of confusion but of peace, so worship must be orderly.

nuance.analogy: Confusion is like a tangled necklace: the strands are all there, but you cannot see which one belongs where.
nuance.etymology: From Latin confundere, to pour together, mix, or confound, from com- 'together' and fundere 'to pour'.
common_mistakes: Using 'confuse' as an adjective instead of 'confused' or 'confusing.'
Stressing the first syllable instead of the second.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word behind 'confuse' in Acts 19:32 is syncheō, meaning to throw into confusion or confound. Acts 19:32 says the assembly in Ephesus was in confusion, with some shouting one thing and some another. 1 Corinthians 14:33 says God is not a God of confusion but of peace.

confuse.etymology: from Middle English *confused* (“frustrated, ruined”), from Anglo-Norman *confus*, from Latin *cōnfūsus*, past participle of *cōnfundō*.

senses.definition: A collection or aggregation of disparate items.

core.definition: A jumbled collection or heap of many different things that are not connected in an orderly way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, KAHN, and pronounce the middle as a reduced 'juh'. The final syllable is a long 'eez' sound, so do not pronounce the ending as 'ees' or add an extra 'ay'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It suggests a collection that is messy, disorganized or hard to make sense of.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'congeries' in everyday speech. It appears in academic writing, literary criticism and historical analysis, usually when describing a set of unrelated things. In professional writing, 'collection' or 'mix' is clearer unless precision is needed.

distinctions.note: 'Collection' implies items chosen or organized together, while 'congeries' stresses that the items are disparate, heaped together and lacking a clear order.
'Aggregate' is a technical term in statistics for a combined total, while 'congeries' is a literary word for a loose heap of different things.

examples.professional: The legacy system is a congeries of scripts, cron jobs and manual exports that nobody fully understands anymore.
examples.analytical: The text presents not a unified doctrine but a congeries of inherited traditions, each reinterpreted in light of the others.

nuance.analogy: A congeries is like a junk drawer: many useful and useless things piled together with no clear arrangement.
nuance.etymology: From Latin congeries, 'a heap, a collection', from congerere, 'to heap together', from con- 'together' and gerere 'to carry, bear'.
common_mistakes: Using 'congeries' as a plural of 'congery' in everyday speech, when most Americans say 'a collection' or 'a mix'.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'kon-JEER-eez'.
Mispronouncing the middle 'ge' as a hard 'g' sound.

congeries.etymology: Latin *congeriēs* (“a heap, mass, pile”), from *congerō* (“to carry together, heap”).

senses.definition: A cluster of heterogeneous things.
A corporation formed by the combination of several smaller corporations whose activities are unrelated to the corporation's primary activity.
A rock consisting of gravel or pebbles embedded in a matrix.
Clustered together into a mass.
senses.example: conglomerate flowers

senses.definition: Made up of heterogeneous elements; composite.
Composed of fragments of rock, pebbles, or stones cemented together.
To combine together into a larger mass.
To combine together into a larger corporation.

core.definition: A large company made up of several smaller companies that operate in unrelated industries under one owner.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, GLAH. The noun ends in a reduced 'ut' sound, while the verb is /kənˈɡlɑməˌreɪt/ with a final 'ayt'. Do not pronounce the middle syllable as a full 'o' like GLOM.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in business contexts. It can sound negative when used to suggest a big, impersonal company that owns too many unrelated businesses.
nuance.usage_note: In business news, Americans use conglomerate for a holding company that owns unrelated businesses, such as a firm with a railroad, a food brand, and a TV network. In casual speech it can also mean any mixed collection of things. The word is common in finance and news but rarely used in personal conversation.

distinctions.note: A corporation is any legal business entity; a conglomerate is a large corporation made up of many unrelated businesses.
A merger joins two companies, often in related fields; a conglomerate usually grows by buying businesses in unrelated fields.

examples.everyday: Did you know the company that makes my cereal is part of a huge conglomerate?
examples.professional: Our parent company is a conglomerate, so the analytics team supports three unrelated businesses.
examples.analytical: A conglomerate's value often depends less on the quality of its parts than on whether headquarters can coordinate them.

nuance.analogy: Like a backpack stuffed with unrelated things, all held together by one zipper.
nuance.etymology: From Latin conglomeratus, past participle of conglomerare, 'to wind into a ball', from com- 'together' and glomus 'ball'.
common_mistakes: Calling any large company a conglomerate; the word specifically means unrelated businesses under one owner.
Using the verb ending -ate for the noun: the noun is kun-GLAH-mer-ut, while the verb ends in -ayt.

senses.definition: To move (something) from one place to another.
senses.example: Air conveys sound. Water is conveyed through the pipe.

senses.definition: To communicate; to make known; to portray.
senses.example: to convey an impression; to convey information

senses.definition: To transfer legal rights (to).
senses.example: He conveyed ownership of the company to his daughter.

senses.definition: (dated) To take or carry (someone) from one place to another.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: To communicate a message, feeling, or idea so that another person understands it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, 'VAY', and make the diphthong clearly as 'ay'. The first syllable is a reduced schwa, so don't say 'kahn' or 'kon'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise, slightly formal word for getting a meaning across.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use convey most often in professional writing and polished speech, as in 'I want to convey my concern.' In casual talk people more often say 'get across,' 'get the point across,' or 'say.' Convey can also mean physically carrying something, though that sense is rarer in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: Say is simple and everyday; convey implies communicating a deeper meaning, mood, or idea beyond the literal words.
Carry is general for moving things; convey is more formal and often refers to messages, meanings, or legal rights.

examples.everyday: I tried to convey how much I appreciated the help, but I was too tired to say it well.
examples.professional: The slide deck needs to convey the key risks to the executives in under five minutes.
examples.analytical: The parable conveys its meaning not through explicit doctrine but through the reversal of expectations in the story.

nuance.analogy: Like a courier carrying a sealed letter: the meaning travels from one person to another.
nuance.etymology: From Anglo-Norman conveier, from Vulgar Latin conviare 'to accompany on the way,' from Latin com- 'with' and via 'way'.
common_mistakes: Using convey as a synonym for 'convince' or 'persuade.'
Saying 'convey about' instead of 'convey' with a direct object, as in 'convey the news.'

convey.etymology: From Middle English *conveien*, from Old French *conveier*, from Vulgar Latin **convio*, from Classical Latin *via* (“way”).

senses.definition: The uncontrolled use of abusive, obscene or scatological language; especially such behavior associated with Tourette syndrome.

core.definition: Involuntary use of obscene or taboo words, most often discussed as a symptom of Tourette syndrome.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on lay. Keep the first vowel as the short ah of cot, and reduce the middle syllables to a quick uh.

nuance.connotation: Clinical and sensitive. It is a neutral medical term, but people with Tourette syndrome often object to its misuse as a stereotype.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use coprolalia mainly in medical, psychological, and educational settings. Many people wrongly think all people with Tourette syndrome have it, so speakers should be careful to note that it affects only a minority. In everyday talk, people usually say swearing or cursing involuntarily.

distinctions.note: Profanity is deliberate swearing; coprolalia is involuntary and often linked to a neurological condition.
Tourette syndrome is the broader condition with many tics; coprolalia is only one possible symptom.

examples.everyday: Many people think Tourette means coprolalia, but most people who have it never swear involuntarily.
examples.professional: The clinic treats tics broadly, and coprolalia affects only a minority of the patients we see.
examples.analytical: Coprolalia is vivid and easily remembered, but its prominence in popular culture distorts public understanding of the condition.

nuance.analogy: Coprolalia is like a sudden burst of static in a radio signal: an unwanted interruption that comes from the wiring, not from the speaker's intention.
nuance.etymology: From Greek kopros, meaning dung, and lalia, meaning speech.
common_mistakes: Placing the stress on the wrong syllable; the main stress is on lay, as in lay.
Assuming all people with Tourette syndrome have coprolalia, which is a common misconception.

senses.definition: A sudden display of brilliance; a flashing of light; a sparkle.

core.definition: A sudden, brilliant flash or sparkle of light; also, a showy display of wit or brilliance in speech or writing.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on SKAY, and the first syllable keeps a clear American r. Do not reduce the middle syllables too much, and avoid confusing this word with corrosion.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes a dazzling display, though it can be used ironically for a showy performance with little substance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use coruscation mainly in literary criticism, essays, and formal writing, and rarely in speech. It is not a word for everyday conversation, so in casual talk you would say sparkle, glint, or flash. Using it in a toast or a formal speech can be effective when you want a vivid image.

distinctions.note: Scintillation refers to many small, rapid flashes, while coruscation describes a brighter, more showy burst of light or wit.
A glint is a single, quick flash, whereas coruscation implies a more vivid and sustained display.
Corrosion is the gradual wearing away of metal, which is a completely different meaning despite the similar spelling.

examples.professional: The keynote's coruscation of slides dazzled the room but left the audience no clearer on the findings.
examples.analytical: Dazzling rhetorical coruscation can conceal an argument as thin as the glitter it borrows.

nuance.analogy: Like a diamond catching the light, coruscation is a quick, brilliant flash that is gone almost as soon as it appears.
nuance.etymology: From Latin coruscare, meaning to glitter or flash.
common_mistakes: Confusing coruscation with corrosion, which is a completely different word.
Using it in casual speech, where sparkle or flash sounds more natural.

senses.definition: A quick, brilliant, and highly successful act.
A coup d'état.
A takeover of one group by another.
A single roll of the wheel at roulette, or a deal in rouge et noir.
One of various named strategies employed by the declarer to win more tricks, such as the Bath coup.
Of Native Americans, a blow against an enemy delivered in a way that demonstrates bravery.
To execute a coup.
To subject (a nation) to a coup d'état.
To empty out, overturn, or tilt, such as from a cart or wheelbarrow.

core.definition: A sudden, successful takeover of power, or a brilliant and surprising achievement that wins an advantage.

pronunciation.tip: Say it as one syllable, like 'coo,' with a long u sound. The word is pronounced differently from 'cup,' so do not add a p sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the political sense is negative, while the achievement sense is positive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use coup for an illegal overthrow of a government in news and history, and for a brilliant achievement in everyday talk, such as 'Landing that client was a real coup.' In the political sense it is often written as 'coup d'état,' and the achievement sense is informal but common in business.

distinctions.note: A revolution is a broad, popular movement to change a system; a coup is usually a quick seizure of power by a small group.
A triumph is a major success that is celebrated; a coup is a surprising, clever success that may be quietly won.

examples.everyday: Getting tickets to the sold-out game was a real coup for my brother.
examples.professional: Signing the largest client of the year was a coup for the sales team.
examples.analytical: The historian argues that the coup was less a sudden seizure than the culmination of a slow erosion of civilian authority.

nuance.analogy: Like a chess move that wins a piece no one expected you to take.
nuance.etymology: From French coup (blow, stroke), from Latin colpus, a blow.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like 'cup,' with a short u and final p.
Using coup for any success; it implies surprise or cleverness, not routine progress.

coup.etymology: Reborrowed in modern times from modern French *coup* (“blow, strike”), from Old French *coup*, from Late Latin *colpus*, from Latin *colaphus*.

senses.definition: The deity that created the world.
Something or someone which creates or makes something.
senses.example: Kenneth E. Iverson was the creator of APL.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of content creator, someone who regularly produces and publishes content on social media, especially of a monetizable nature.
senses.example: creator economy

senses.definition: A player who creates opportunities for their team to score goals; a playmaker.

core.definition: God, understood as the one who made the universe and everything in it, usually written with a capital C.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, 'ay', and pronounce the middle t as a quick American flap, like the d in 'ladder'. The final 'or' is a weak rhotic vowel, so say 'ter', not 'tor'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to reverent when used for God; neutral when used for a person or a creative source.
nuance.usage_note: In American religious speech, Creator usually refers to God and is capitalized, especially in prayers, hymns, and sermons. In everyday speech, creator can mean a person who makes something, such as an artist or inventor, or a content creator on social media. A natural reply to a compliment about your work is 'Thanks, I had a lot of fun making it.'

distinctions.note: Maker is more casual and concrete, while creator is more formal and can suggest original invention or artistic origin.
Author usually refers to someone who writes a text, while creator can apply to any kind of original work or invention.

examples.everyday: My grandmother always says that every sunrise is a gift from the Creator.
examples.professional: As the creator of this dashboard, I can walk the team through how the metrics are calculated.
examples.analytical: The Christian doctrine of God as Creator distinguishes the divine source of all being from the finite beings that depend on it.

nuance.analogy: A creator is like a potter whose hands shape the clay into a form that did not exist before.
nuance.etymology: From Latin creator, from creare, to create.
common_mistakes: Using lowercase creator when referring to God in a religious context, where Americans usually capitalize it.
Stressing the first syllable; the stress is on the second syllable, 'ay'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew verb bara means to create and is used in Genesis 1:1 with God as the subject. In Greek, ktisis refers to creation and the creature, and the New Testament uses related terms when speaking of God as Maker. Romans 1:25 contrasts worshiping the creature with worshiping the Creator. Ecclesiastes 12:1 urges the reader to remember the Creator in youth.

creator.etymology: From Middle English *creatour*, from Old French *creator*, *creatur*, *creatour*, from Latin *creātor*, agent noun from perfect passive participle *creātus* (“created”), from verb *creō* (“to create”) + agent suffix *-or*.

senses.definition: A gradual increase of anything, especially to a dramatic climax.
senses.example: Their fighting rose in a fearsome crescendo.

senses.definition: An instruction to play gradually more loudly, denoted by a long, narrow angle with its apex on the left ( < ), by musicians called a hairpin.
To increase in intensity; to reach or head for a crescendo.
senses.example: The band crescendoed and then suddenly went silent.

senses.definition: Gradually increasing in force or loudness.

core.definition: A gradual increase in loudness, intensity or energy, often building toward a dramatic climax.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, SHEN, and the final syllable is a long O. Do not pronounce the 'sc' as 'sk'; it is a 'sh' sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive or dramatic, suggesting excitement, building energy or an approaching climax. It can also describe a worsening situation, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'crescendo' in music, sports, news and everyday talk about a build-up of noise or emotion, such as a crowd cheering louder before a goal. It is a fairly common word in American speech and writing. Used for a bad situation, it implies a dramatic peak of trouble.

distinctions.note: A crescendo is the gradual buildup to the peak, while a climax is the highest point itself.
A diminuendo is a gradual decrease in volume, the opposite of a crescendo.

examples.everyday: The crowd's cheering reached a crescendo when our team scored the winning goal in the last minute.
examples.professional: Our sprint ended in a crescendo of late bug reports, so we need a better testing schedule next quarter.
examples.analytical: The novel's argument builds to a crescendo in which every earlier theme returns in a single, unresolved climax.

nuance.analogy: A crescendo is like a wave rising toward the shore: the energy keeps gathering until it breaks.
nuance.etymology: From Italian crescendo, the present participle of crescere, meaning to grow, from Latin crescere.
common_mistakes: Saying 'crescendo' for a sudden loud noise; it means a gradual increase toward a peak.
Mispronouncing the 'sc' as 'sk' rather than 'sh.'

crescendo.etymology: Italian *crescendo*, gerund of *crescere* (“to grow, to increase”).

senses.definition: In accordance with, or established by, custom or common usage.
Holding or held by custom.
senses.example: customary tenants

senses.definition: A book containing laws and usages, or customs; a custumal.

core.definition: Done, used or accepted as a usual practice or tradition in a group or society.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final '-ary' is a reduced 'ee' sound, not a full 'ah-ree'. The middle 'tə' is a quick schwa; avoid saying 'CUS-tom-ary' with a strong 'o'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; describes accepted practice without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this adjective in formal writing, legal documents, and academic discussions of tradition. In casual talk they say 'usual' or 'normal' instead. For example, 'It's customary to tip' sounds fine, while 'It's our customary dinner spot' is more natural as 'our usual spot.'

distinctions.note: Usual is everyday and frequent; customary emphasizes tradition or social convention.
Traditional refers to long-established cultural forms; customary refers to accepted practice in a specific setting.

examples.everyday: It's customary to bring a small gift when you're invited to someone's house for dinner.
examples.professional: Our team's customary approach is to review pull requests within 24 hours before merging them.
examples.analytical: Customary law, unlike statutory law, derives its authority from long-standing community practice rather than written enactment.

nuance.analogy: Like an unwritten house rule that everyone follows because 'that's how we've always done it.'
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin consuetudinarius, from Latin consuetudo, 'custom.'
common_mistakes: Using 'customary' in casual speech, where 'usual' sounds more natural.
Confusing the adjective with the noun 'custom' in plural form.
patterns: it is customary (for sb) to do sth

customary.etymology: From Middle English *custumary*, from Medieval Latin *custumarius*.

senses.definition: The state or quality of being deceitful; duplicity.

core.definition: The quality or habit of being deceitful; a tendency to mislead others or hide the truth.

pronunciation.tip: Stress SEET, the second syllable, and reduce the ending to 'fuhl-nuss.' The final 'ness' is a short 's' sound, not 'nes' with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a character trait of dishonesty and misleading others.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use deceitfulness in formal writing, religious writing, and discussions of character, usually to describe a general quality rather than one lie. In everyday speech they would usually say 'dishonesty' or 'being fake.' It is often paired with words like 'pride' or 'wickedness' in moral and religious contexts.

distinctions.note: Dishonesty is the general everyday term for not telling the truth, while deceitfulness emphasizes a persistent character trait of misleading others.
Deception is an act or process of misleading, while deceitfulness is the underlying quality that makes someone prone to it.

examples.everyday: After years of his deceitfulness, I finally stopped trusting anything he told me about money.
examples.professional: The manager's deceitfulness in the reports eroded the team's confidence, and HR had to step in.
examples.analytical: Theologians have long argued that the deceitfulness of sin lies in its power to disguise itself as good, which makes self-examination difficult.

nuance.analogy: Deceitfulness is like a foggy window: it does not always show a clear lie, but it keeps you from seeing what is really there.
nuance.etymology: From deceitful plus -ness, from Old French deceite, from Latin decipere (to ensnare).
common_mistakes: Using deceitfulness for a single lie; it describes a general quality, so 'a lie' or 'deceit' is better for one act.
Confusing the noun deceitfulness with the adjective deceitful in a sentence.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew and Greek words for deceit describe a condition of the heart and speech, not only a single act of lying. Jeremiah 17:9 warns that the heart is deceitful above all things, which points to the inward roots of dishonesty. Mark 7:22 lists deceit among the evils that come from within a person, and it appears among the sins that defile a person.

senses.definition: In a definable manner; identifiably.

core.definition: In a way that can be clearly identified, described, or recognized.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FY, which rhymes with "sky." The final syllable is "blee," not "bul" with a long a.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes something that can be clearly identified or measured, without a positive or negative tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "definably" mainly in academic, technical, or formal writing when precision matters. In everyday speech, people say "clearly," "noticeably," or "distinctly" instead. Most Americans would find "definably" slightly stiff in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: "Clearly" is common in everyday speech and means easy to see or understand. "Definably" stresses that something can be specifically identified or measured.
"Distinctly" emphasizes a sharp, noticeable difference. "Definably" focuses on whether something can be pinned down or categorized.

examples.everyday: The new coffee tastes definably better than the old one, so I'm switching brands.
examples.professional: The model's accuracy improved definably after we removed the duplicate records from the training set.
examples.analytical: A concept is definably theological when its content can be stated in terms of God's nature, acts, or revealed will.

nuance.analogy: Something definably different is like a photo with a clear outline: you can point to the edge and say exactly where it begins.
nuance.etymology: From definable (from define, from Latin definire, "to limit") plus the adverbial suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as "bul" in the adverb form, when it should be "blee."
Using "definably" in casual speech where "clearly" sounds more natural.

senses.definition: Intentionally, or after deliberation; not accidentally.
senses.example: He deliberately broke that, didn't he?

senses.definition: Taking one's time, slowly and carefully.
senses.example: After being called upon, he strode deliberately up to the blackboard.

core.definition: On purpose, intentionally, not by accident; or in a slow, careful, and unhurried way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LIB, and the final -ly is pronounced lee. Many learners add an extra syllable after the b, so say the middle as er, not uh-rayt.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can sound negative when it describes someone intentionally causing trouble, and positive when it describes careful, measured action.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say deliberately in everyday speech to mean on purpose, as in he deliberately ignored me. It is often used to emphasize that something was not an accident. In a positive sense, you can say she spoke deliberately, meaning slowly and carefully.

distinctions.note: Intentionally is more neutral and slightly more formal. Deliberately often carries a sense of conscious choice, sometimes with blame.
On purpose is the most common everyday phrase in conversation. Deliberately is a bit more formal or emphatic.

examples.everyday: I didn't forget your birthday; I deliberately waited to surprise you.
examples.professional: We deliberately kept the rollout small so we could catch problems early.
examples.analytical: The text deliberately withholds information, forcing the reader to infer the motive behind the character's silence.

nuance.analogy: Like a painter who places each brushstroke with intent rather than letting paint drip at random.
nuance.etymology: From deliberate (adjective) plus the adverbial suffix -ly, ultimately from Latin deliberare (to weigh carefully).
common_mistakes: Using deliberately for things that were simply slow or careful without intent, where carefully is more natural.
Mispronouncing it with an extra syllable, saying dih-LIB-er-ate-lee.

senses.definition: Perverted or extremely wrong in a moral sense.
senses.example: a depraved killer

senses.definition: Violating principles of rectitude or given standards of decency.

core.definition: Morally corrupt or wicked, showing a complete lack of decency or moral principle.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on PRAYVD, and the final sound is a single d after v, so 'depraved' is one syllable after the stressed one, not two. The r is strongly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It condemns someone's moral character and is used for serious crimes or cruelty.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'depraved' in news about violent crimes, in moral criticism, and in church preaching. It is strong, so it should be used carefully and not for minor offenses. In casual talk, people might say 'twisted' or 'sick', though those words are less formal.

distinctions.note: Evil describes morally wrong acts or forces broadly; depraved emphasizes corruption of character or a complete loss of decency.
Wicked is more common and can be playful; depraved is stronger and more serious.

examples.everyday: The news about that crime was so awful that my neighbor just said it was depraved.
examples.professional: The compliance report described the executives' conduct as depraved, which led to immediate firings.
examples.analytical: The moralist asks whether a depraved act can be understood without condemning the agent entirely.

nuance.analogy: Like a fruit that has rotted through so that nothing edible is left in it.
nuance.etymology: From the past participle of Latin depravare, 'to distort, pervert'.
common_mistakes: Using 'depraved' for mild misbehavior, which sounds exaggerated.
Confusing the adjective 'depraved' with the noun 'depravity'.
nuance.biblical_note: Romans 1:28 in the RSV speaks of God giving people up to a base mind, and the Greek word adokimos means 'unfit' or 'reprobate', not fit for proper judgment. Genesis 6:5 describes the wickedness of human hearts before the flood, using Hebrew words for evil inclination and thought. These passages support the biblical picture of human moral corruption.

senses.definition: Willful neglect of one's duty.
senses.example: The new soldier did not clean his cabin and was scolded for dereliction and disobedience.

senses.definition: The act of abandoning something, or the state of being abandoned.
Land gained from the water by a change of water-line.

core.definition: Failure to do what one is responsible for, especially neglect of a clear duty, as in dereliction of duty.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on LIK, with a lighter secondary stress on DAIR. The -tion ending is shun, and the r is clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it implies blame, often for a serious failure of responsibility.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dereliction mostly in set phrases like dereliction of duty, which appear in news about officials, police, or military personnel. In everyday talk people would say neglecting your duties or slacking off. Saying it lightly about a small mistake sounds overly dramatic.

distinctions.note: Negligence is failure to take reasonable care, often without intent; dereliction usually implies a conscious or serious failure of duty.
Neglect is the general act of not caring for something; dereliction is more formal and tied to a specific duty.

examples.everyday: My neighbor thinks the city's dereliction of duty is why the potholes never get fixed.
examples.professional: The auditor documented a clear dereliction of duty when the approval steps were skipped for the payment system.
examples.analytical: Kant would ask whether the official's dereliction violated a duty that holds regardless of consequences.

nuance.analogy: Like a lifeguard who looks at his phone while someone is drowning: the job was his, and he simply stopped doing it.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin derelictio, from derelinquere, to abandon completely, from de- plus relinquere, to leave.
common_mistakes: Using dereliction for a small slip; it implies serious neglect.
Misspelling it as derilection or confusing it with derelict as a noun in the phrase dereliction of duty.

dereliction.etymology: From Latin *dērelictiō* (“neglect, abandonment”), from *dērelinquō* (“to neglect, abandon”), from *dē-* + *re-* + *linquō* (“to leave”).

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to dialectic; logically reasoned through the exchange of opposing ideas.
Synonym of dialectal (“of or pertaining to a dialect”).

core.definition: Relating to dialectic; reasoning by weighing opposing ideas to reach a fuller, more adequate truth.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LEK, the third syllable. The final '-ical' is quick and reduced to 'kul', so do not say a full 'ih-cal'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive in academic and philosophical writing. It can sound jargon-heavy in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dialectical in philosophy, theology and political writing, often with method, tension or thinking. Many people also know it from dialectical behavior therapy (DBT), a therapy that balances acceptance with change. In everyday speech, 'two-sided' or 'back and forth' is more natural.

distinctions.note: Dialectical concerns argument and reasoning, while dialectal concerns regional forms of language.
Logical refers to valid inference, while dialectical adds opposition and resolution of contradictions.
Argumentative means inclined to dispute, while dialectical describes a disciplined method of reasoning.

examples.everyday: My therapist uses dialectical behavior therapy, which helps me accept myself while still working on change.
examples.professional: Our team took a dialectical approach, weighing speed against reliability until we found a workable compromise.
examples.analytical: Kierkegaard's dialectical method refuses to resolve the tension between faith and reason into a neat system.

nuance.analogy: Like a suspension bridge held up by opposing cables, where the tension on each side keeps the structure standing.
nuance.etymology: From Latin dialecticus, from Greek dialektikos 'of conversation', from dialegesthai 'to converse'.
common_mistakes: Confusing dialectical (relating to argument) with dialectal (relating to dialect).
Using dialectical as a casual synonym for 'two-sided'; it implies a structured method of reasoning.

senses.definition: That which directs; serving to direct, indicate, or guide.
Relating to the directive case.
An instruction or guideline that indicates how to perform an action or reach a goal.
A construct in source code that indicates how it should be processed but is not necessarily part of the program to be run.
An authoritative decision from an official body, which may or may not have binding force.
The directive case.
A form of legislative act addressed to the member states. The directive binds the member state to reach certain objectives in their national legislation.

core.definition: An official instruction or guideline from a manager, organization, or authority that tells people how to act or what to do.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on REK, and the first syllable is a weak uh. Americans clearly pronounce the r, and the final syllable is a short -iv, not -eeve.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative; a directive can sound bureaucratic or controlling depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: In American workplaces and government, directive is used for a formal instruction, often from higher management or a federal agency. Saying 'We got a directive from corporate' sounds official. In casual talk, people say order, rule, or instruction. The adjective is less common, but people say directive language or directive style.

distinctions.note: A directive is binding and comes from authority; a guideline is advisory and suggests good practice.
Order is more blunt and informal; directive sounds formal and written, often from an official source.

examples.everyday: My landlord sent a directive about parking, so now we all have to use the back lot.
examples.professional: The compliance team issued a new directive requiring all data access requests to go through the review queue.
examples.analytical: Scripture is often read as a directive for conduct, but its narrative forms also shape moral imagination in ways a rule does not.

nuance.analogy: A directive is like a road sign that says 'one way'; it is an official instruction you are expected to follow.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin directivus, from Latin dirigere, to direct.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as -eeve instead of a short -iv
Using directive as a common everyday word for any instruction, when it sounds formal and official

senses.definition: The loss of confidence or enthusiasm.
The act of discouraging.
Anything that discourages.

core.definition: A feeling of lost hope or confidence, or something that makes people lose hope or motivation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress SKUR. Pronounce the middle -ij- as a short syllable, and make the last syllable -ment a weak, reduced sound, muhnt.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a loss of hope or a discouraging force, often in serious or reflective contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use discouragement in writing, speeches, and conversations about difficult times. In casual talk, people often say it was discouraging or I felt discouraged. The word can also describe a thing, as in The delay was a real discouragement to the team.

distinctions.note: Disappointment is a sad feeling when something does not happen as expected; discouragement is a loss of hope or motivation that can last longer.
Despair is a very deep loss of hope; discouragement is usually milder and more temporary.

examples.everyday: After three rejections, I felt a real sense of discouragement, but my friends kept me going.
examples.professional: The slow approval process has been a constant source of discouragement for the design team.
examples.analytical: Some Puritan writers saw spiritual discouragement as a test of faith rather than evidence of God's absence.

nuance.analogy: Discouragement is like fog on a trail: it does not stop you, but it makes every step harder to see.
nuance.etymology: From discourage plus the suffix -ment, meaning the result or state of an action.
common_mistakes: Using discouragement as a verb.
Using discouragement when you mean the action of persuading someone not to do something, which is usually expressed as advice against something.

senses.definition: Available at one's discretion; able to be used as one chooses; left to or regulated by one's own discretion or judgment.
senses.example: discretionary income

core.definition: Left to a person's own judgment or choice rather than fixed by rules; optional.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KREH, with a weaker secondary stress on NEH in the -ary ending, which is pronounced 'eh-ree'. Do not give every syllable equal weight.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it describes a choice that is not required.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use discretionary in finance, government and HR, as in 'discretionary spending,' 'discretionary income' or 'discretionary budget.' It means not required by law or policy. In casual talk, people say 'optional' or 'extra.'

distinctions.note: Optional is everyday and general; discretionary is formal and implies a decision left to someone's judgment, often in budgets or rules.
Mandatory means required; discretionary means left to choice, so the two are close opposites in policy language.

examples.everyday: After rent and groceries, I have a little discretionary income left for fun.
examples.professional: We'll keep discretionary spending on conferences low until the quarter closes.
examples.analytical: Courts often rely on discretionary authority, which makes their reasoning harder to predict from the text of the statute.

nuance.analogy: Like free time on a calendar: nothing forces you to fill it, but you choose how to use it.
nuance.etymology: From discretion plus -ary, relating to discretion.
common_mistakes: Misplacing the stress, saying disKREH-shuh-ree with the secondary stress lost.
Confusing discretionary with discreet, which is about tact rather than choice.

senses.definition: To remove or force out from a position or dwelling previously occupied.
To move or go from a dwelling or former position.
To force out of a secure or settled position.

core.definition: To force or knock something out of a place where it was firmly stuck, fixed, or settled.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, LODGE, and the vowel is the open American 'ah' sound, so it rhymes with 'dodge'. Do not add an extra syllable at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a physical or political action without judging it, though it implies that the thing resisted moving.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dislodge for removing something stuck, such as a clogged drain blockage, a stone wedged in a tire, or a politician from office. For something simply taken away, Americans more often say remove or get rid of. A natural reply to 'Did you dislodge it?' is 'Yes, it finally came loose.'

distinctions.note: Remove is general and neutral. Dislodge implies the object was firmly fixed or lodged and had to be forced loose.
Oust means to force someone out of a position or office, often by a formal or political process. Dislodge is more physical and can apply to objects.

examples.everyday: The plumber used a long wire to dislodge the clog in the kitchen sink.
examples.professional: We need a stronger adhesive so the sensor won't dislodge when the vibration motor runs.
examples.analytical: The reform movement sought to dislodge entrenched interests that had long controlled local patronage networks.

nuance.analogy: Like prying a stuck jar lid loose with a spoon: the object was lodged in place and you had to force it out.
nuance.etymology: From Old French deslogier, to remove from lodging, from des- (away) and loge (lodging).
common_mistakes: Using dislodge for simple removal without force, as in 'dislodge the trash' instead of 'take out the trash'.
Stressing the first syllable (DIS-lodge) instead of the second.

dislodge.etymology: From Middle English *disloggen*, from Old French *deslogier*.

senses.definition: An electronic screen that shows graphics or text.
A show or spectacle.
senses.example: The trapeze artist put on an amazing acrobatic display.

senses.definition: A piece of work to be presented visually.
senses.example: Pupils are expected to produce a wall display about a country of their choice.

senses.definition: A device, furniture or marketing-oriented bulk packaging for visual presentation for sales promotion.
The presentation of information for visual or tactile reception.
To show conspicuously; to exhibit; to demonstrate; to manifest.
To make a display; to act as one making a show or demonstration.
To extend the front of (a column), bringing it into line, deploy.
(dated) To make conspicuous by using large or prominent type.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: An arrangement of items to be seen, such as in a store, or a screen that shows images or text.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PLAY, with a long a sound. In everyday American speech the word is clearly two syllables, and the final y is a long ee sound that is often softened in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use display very often in shopping, technology, and everyday descriptions, such as a window display or a phone display. As a noun it is neutral and common, though a 'display' of emotion can sound dramatic. In casual speech people often say 'screen' for a phone or monitor, and 'shelf' or 'window' for a store arrangement.

distinctions.note: Exhibit is more formal and suggests an organized showing, often in a museum or gallery; display is more everyday and can be a simple arrangement.
Screen is the everyday word for the surface you look at on a device; display is the more technical or product-description term.

examples.everyday: The store has a big holiday display near the front, so you cannot miss the cookies.
examples.professional: The new dashboard display shows the conversion rate in real time, which makes the team's weekly review much faster.
examples.analytical: Goffman's dramaturgical model treats everyday self-presentation as a display in which the person manages the impression given to others.

nuance.analogy: Like a painting hung on a wall, a display puts something where people can see it clearly.
nuance.etymology: From Old French despleier, 'to unfold', from Latin displicare, 'to scatter, unfold'.
common_mistakes: Using display as a verb with the wrong preposition; say 'display on' a shelf or 'on display', not 'display in' when you mean being shown publicly.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the second.

display.etymology: From Middle English *displayen*, from Anglo-Norman *despleier* and Old French *despleier*, *desploiier*, from Medieval Latin *displicare* (“to unfold, display”), from Latin *dis-* (“apart”) + *plicāre* (“to fold”).

conversation.text: I love the lamp on display in the window. Is it for sale?
Sorry, that one's just for display, but we have new ones in the back.
The display on this laptop is so much brighter than my old one.

senses.definition: To convince not to try or do.
senses.example: Jane dissuaded Martha from committing suicide.

core.definition: To persuade someone not to do something, usually by giving reasons or warnings.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, and the -suade sounds like swayd. Do not pronounce the s as a z or add an extra vowel between the s and w.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes advising or convincing someone against an action, and can sound a bit formal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dissuade in news, legal discussion, and polite advice, but more often say talk out of or talk him out of it in casual conversation. It is usually followed by from plus a noun or -ing form. If you are trying to stop a friend, say try to talk you out of it or convince you not to.

distinctions.note: Persuade means to cause someone to do something; dissuade means to cause someone not to do it.
Deter means to discourage through fear or consequences, while dissuade means to convince someone through reasons or argument.

examples.everyday: My sister tried to dissuade me from buying a used car, but I bought it anyway.
examples.professional: Legal will try to dissuade the team from signing the contract before the security review is done.
examples.analytical: Aristotle distinguishes between arguments that persuade and arguments that dissuade, showing how both depend on the listener's judgment.

nuance.analogy: To dissuade someone is like gently closing a door they were about to walk through.
nuance.etymology: From Latin dissuadere, from dis- (apart) and suadere (to advise or persuade).
common_mistakes: Using dissuade to, as in dissuade him to leave; the correct pattern is dissuade someone from doing something.
Confusing dissuade with persuade, which points in the opposite direction.

dissuade.etymology: From Middle French *dissuader*, from Latin *dissuādeō* (“to urge differently”, “to advise against”, “to dissuade”), from *dis-* (“away from”, “asunder”) + *suādeō* (“to recommend”, “to advise”, “to urge”).

senses.definition: The act or an instance of dissuading.

core.definition: The act of persuading someone not to do something, or the argument used to do so.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable -SWAY-, and the -sion ending is pronounced zhun.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly formal. It describes an argument or effort against an action.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use dissuasion in everyday speech and almost never in casual talk. You will see it more in legal, political, or literary writing, where persuasion and dissuasion are discussed. In daily conversation, people use talking someone out of it, warning, or advice.

distinctions.note: Persuasion is the act of encouraging someone to do something; dissuasion is the act of encouraging them not to.
Deterrence focuses on preventing action through threat or cost, while dissuasion focuses on argument, reasons, or advice.

examples.everyday: Her friends made some strong dissuasion before she quit her job, but she went ahead.
examples.professional: The vendor's dissuasion memo argued against changing the database, but the team still chose to move.
examples.analytical: Socrates' dissuasion of the young man from ambition is less a rejection of desire than a call to examine its source.

nuance.analogy: Dissuasion is like a traffic sign that says do not enter: it steers people away without forcing them.
nuance.etymology: From Latin dissuasio, from dissuadere, meaning to advise against.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in dih-SWAY-zhun versus DIS-uh-zhun.
Using dissuasion as a verb, when the verb is dissuade.

dissuasion.etymology: From Middle English *dissuasioun*, from Middle French *dissuasion*.

core.definition: In the Bible, a place near Bethlehem, or a Levite, named in Genesis and Micah; from the Hebrew word for flock.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, EE. The second syllable is a reduced American er, so say it as one light syllable at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a proper name and has no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Most Americans will only meet Eder in Bible study or as a personal name. In a sermon or Bible study, say EE-der for the place and the Levite. Outside those settings, it is rarely used in ordinary conversation.

distinctions.note: Eden is the paradise garden in Genesis; Eder is a different place name meaning tower or flock, and the two are not related in meaning.

examples.everyday: My Bible study group got stuck on the name Eder, and someone asked whether it was a place or a person.
examples.professional: In the commentary, the section on Eder explains how the tower of the flock relates to Bethlehem's pastoral history.
examples.analytical: Micah 4:8 uses the tower of the flock, Migdal-eder, as an image of a restored Jerusalem, and that reading depends on the Hebrew term for flock.

nuance.analogy: Like a name on a map that is both a village and a shepherd's watch tower, Eder points to a place and a pastoral purpose at once.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew ʿēder, meaning flock, as in the phrase migdal-ʿēder, tower of the flock.
common_mistakes: Confusing Eder with Eden, which is a different name with a different meaning.
Stressing the second syllable; the stress is on the first.
nuance.biblical_note: Eder appears in several places in the Hebrew Bible. Genesis 35:21 mentions the tower of Eder, a site near Bethlehem, where Jacob pitched his tent after Rachel died. Micah 4:8 speaks of the tower of the flock, Migdal-eder, as a symbol of restored rule for Jerusalem. The Hebrew word means flock, and the name ties the place to shepherding and to Bethlehem, the town associated with David's shepherd origins.

senses.definition: The cardinal number immediately following eighty-one and preceding eighty-three.

core.definition: The cardinal number 82, one more than eighty-one and one less than eighty-three.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TOO, and the word ends with a long oo sound. Do not say 'tuh' or 'two' with a short vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a plain number with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say eighty-two for ages, years and counts. In speech, the final sound is the long oo of 'two', so don't confuse it with 'eighty-too' in a rushed phrase. Hyphenate in writing.

distinctions.note: Eighty-two is the number 82, while eight-two is not a standard form. Write the word 'eighty' in full.

examples.everyday: My mom just turned eighty-two, and she still beats me at cards.
examples.professional: Eighty-two percent of the users completed onboarding without contacting support.
examples.analytical: Eighty-two is two times forty-one, so its only divisors are one, two, forty-one and eighty-two.

nuance.analogy: Eighty-two is like a page number that comes right after eighty-one in a book.
nuance.etymology: Formed from eighty plus two; eighty comes from Old English 'eahtatig', meaning eight tens, and two is Old English 'tu' or 'twa'.
common_mistakes: Saying the final syllable as a short 'tuh' rather than the long TOO.
Writing 'eight-two' or 'eighty two' without a hyphen in formal writing.

senses.definition: Basic, fundamental or elementary.
Of the ancient supposed elements of earth, air, fire and water.
Of, or relating to a force of nature, especially to severe atmospheric conditions.
Comparable to a force of nature; sudden and unpredictable.
Of, relating to, or being an element (as opposed to a compound).

A creature (usually a spirit) that is attuned with, or composed of, one of the classical elements: air, earth, fire and water or variations of them like ice, lightning, etc. They sometimes have unique proper names and sometimes are referred to as Air, Earth, Fire, or Water.

core.definition: Basic and fundamental, forming the essential core of something; also relating to powerful forces of nature, such as wind, fire or storms.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on MEN, with a light secondary stress on the first syllable. The final syllable is a reduced schwa-l, so it sounds like 'tul' and not 'tal'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when describing basic needs or truths, and dramatic when describing nature's power.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use elemental to describe something primal or essential, such as elemental human needs or an elemental truth. In casual speech, people more often say basic or fundamental. Describing weather as elemental sounds literary and slightly dramatic, so it works best in writing or a vivid story.

distinctions.note: Elementary means simple or introductory, as in elementary statistics. Elemental means primal or essential, as in an elemental fear of the dark.
Fundamental is the everyday, neutral word for basic or underlying. Elemental adds a sense of raw, natural force or primal essence.

examples.everyday: Trying to stay warm in a snowstorm brings out something elemental in people.
examples.professional: Before we redesign the dashboard, we need to agree on the elemental metrics every team tracks.
examples.analytical: Kant's argument aims to uncover the elemental structures of human reason that make experience possible.

nuance.analogy: Like the bedrock under a city, elemental things are hidden beneath everything else but hold it all up.
nuance.etymology: From Latin elementum, meaning a first principle or basic substance.
common_mistakes: Confusing elemental with elementary, which means simple or introductory.
Stressing the first syllable instead of MEN.

senses.definition: To enclose objects in a common interface in a way that makes them interchangeable, and guards their states from invalid changes.
To enclose something in, or as if in, a capsule.
To epitomize something by expressing it as a brief summary.
To enclose data in packets that can be transmitted using a given protocol.

core.definition: In software, to hide an object's internal data and methods behind a defined interface so other code can use only approved access.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on KAP, the second syllable. The final -ate is pronounced 'ayt', with the secondary stress on layt.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term, and in general speech it sounds professional or academic.
nuance.usage_note: In American software and data work, engineers say 'encapsulate the state' or 'encapsulate the logic' in a class or module. Outside technical settings, Americans also use it to mean summarize briefly, as in 'the slogan encapsulates the campaign.' In meetings, it is a clear, professional word.

distinctions.note: Summarize means to give the main points briefly; encapsulate suggests that a short statement fully captures the essence of something larger.
Include means to contain as one part; encapsulate means to enclose or capture the whole essence, often in a protective way.

examples.everyday: That one sentence really encapsulates why my grandmother loved that town.
examples.professional: The class encapsulates the database connection so the rest of the team cannot change it directly.
examples.analytical: Aristotle's definition of virtue encapsulates the idea that character is formed through habitual action.

nuance.analogy: Like a pill with a coating: the medicine inside is protected, and you interact with it only through the outside shell.
nuance.etymology: From 'capsule' (a small container), from Latin 'capsula', the diminutive of 'capsa' (box).
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable as en-cap-SU-late; the stress is on KAP.
Confusing the verb with the noun: say 'encapsulation' for the noun, not 'encapsulate' for the process.

senses.definition: The area of a convent or monastery where access is restricted to community members.
Something that is enclosed.
senses.example: He faced punishment for creating the fenced enclosure in a public park.

senses.definition: An area or domain partially or entirely separated or surrounded by barriers.
senses.example: He faced punishment for creating the fenced enclosure in a public park.

senses.definition: Something that is inserted into a letter or similar package.
senses.example: There was an enclosure with the letter — a photo.

senses.definition: The act or process of enclosing something.
senses.example: The experiment requires the enclosure o mercury vapor in a glass tube.

senses.definition: The act or process of separating and surrounding an area or domain with a barrier.
senses.example: The enclosure of public land is against the law.

senses.definition: The insertion or inclusion of an item in a letter or package.
senses.example: The enclosure of a photo with your letter is appreciated.

senses.definition: The act of restricting access to ideas, works of art, or technologies using patents or intellectual property laws.
(historical) The post-feudal process of subdivision of common lands for individual ownership.
senses.example: Strip-farming disappeared after enclosure.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: An area surrounded by a fence, wall or other barrier, such as a pen for animals or a fenced yard; also an item sent inside a letter.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KLOH. The ending -ure is pronounced 'zhur' with a reduced vowel and a clear American r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a plain descriptive word for a space or item.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday talk Americans use enclosure for a fenced space, such as a dog enclosure or a zoo enclosure. In business letters, 'Enclosures:' is a standard heading that lists attached documents. In formal religious contexts it refers to a cloistered space in a monastery.

distinctions.note: A fence is one kind of barrier, while an enclosure is any space surrounded by a barrier.
A pen is a small enclosure for animals, while enclosure can describe a larger or more general area.

examples.everyday: We keep the dogs in the enclosure behind the garage when we go out.
examples.professional: Please see the enclosures listed at the bottom of the letter: the signed agreement and two invoices.
examples.analytical: The monastery's enclosure separates the cloistered community from the outside world and marks its spiritual boundary.

nuance.analogy: A fenced yard is a small world with a wall drawn around it.
nuance.etymology: From Old French 'enclos', from Latin 'includere' (to shut in), with the English suffix '-ure'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'enclosure' with 'closure'; enclosure names the space or the item, not the act of closing.
Stressing the last syllable as 'zhur' with extra emphasis; the stress belongs on KLOH.

senses.definition: In an endearing manner.

core.definition: In a way that makes people feel affection or fondness for someone.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on DEER. Keep the 'ing' short and the final -ly clear as 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes behavior that makes someone seem sweet or lovable.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use endearingly to describe how someone acts or speaks, often in a review, a story or friendly talk. It usually follows a verb, as in 'smiled endearingly' or 'said endearingly.' It is warm but not very informal, so it is more common in writing than in quick speech.

distinctions.note: Sweetly stresses kindness or gentleness, while endearingly stresses the quality that makes someone lovable.
Charmingly suggests social polish and delight, whereas endearingly suggests a more innocent or unguarded warmth.

examples.everyday: He apologized endearingly for burning the pancakes, and we all laughed.
examples.professional: She endearingly admitted that she had never used the new dashboard before the demo.
