examples.analytical: The narrator endearingly undercuts his own authority, which makes his claims more persuasive.

nuance.analogy: Like a friend who hands you a coffee exactly the way you like it, without making a fuss.
nuance.etymology: From 'endearing' (from 'endear') plus the adverb suffix '-ly'.
common_mistakes: Using endearingly for a neutral action, when it should describe something warm or lovable.
Stressing the final syllable instead of DEER.

senses.definition: The act or quality of endorsing.
senses.example: The association announced its endorsement of the policy.

senses.definition: An amendment or annotation to an insurance contract or other official document (such as a driving license).
senses.example: Mr. Jones paid extra for the flood damage endorsement on his house insurance.

senses.definition: An instructor's signed acknowledgement of time practising specific flying skills.
senses.example: Once she obtained the endorsement of her night flying hours, Joanna was approved to take the pilot's examination.

senses.definition: Permission to carry out a specific skill or application in a field in which the practitioner already has a general license.
senses.example: Wanted: Accredited teacher with Grade 12 mathematics endorsement.

senses.definition: Sponsorship, in means of money, by a company, business or enterprise.
senses.example: After the Olympics, he was hoping to get an endorsement deal.

senses.definition: Support from an important, renowned figure of a media (celebrity, politics, sports, etc.), to get back up.
senses.example: I'm not sure whether an endorsement from Donald Trump will help or hurt.

core.definition: A public statement or sign of support for a person, product or idea, often given in exchange for money or influence.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the DORS syllable. The final -ment is weak, so say it as one quick unstressed syllable, not 'men-tuh'.

nuance.connotation: Positive in general, though it can suggest paid influence when used about celebrities.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use endorsement for celebrity ads, political support and professional recommendations, such as 'a strong endorsement from her professor'. The insurance and driver's license senses are specialized. Informally, people might say 'a plug' for free promotion, but endorsement is the standard word.

distinctions.note: A general suggestion; an endorsement is usually more public or formal approval.
Sponsorship is financial support, often for an event; an endorsement is approval, sometimes paid.

examples.everyday: That shampoo got a big endorsement from my favorite singer, so I bought it.
examples.professional: Her manager gave the project a strong endorsement, which helped us get budget approval.
examples.analytical: An endorsement tells us less about truth than about the speaker's willingness to be associated with a claim.

nuance.analogy: An endorsement is like a reference letter: your name is attached to someone else's claim.
nuance.etymology: From endorse plus -ment, via Anglo-French from Latin dorsum 'back'.
common_mistakes: Using 'endorsement' as a verb; the verb is 'endorse'.
Saying 'give an endorsement for' in casual talk; 'endorse someone' or 'give someone an endorsement' is more natural.

senses.definition: To keep up, impose or bring into effect something, not necessarily by force.
senses.example: The police are there to enforce the law.

senses.definition: To apply a rule or enforcement action to a person or user account.
senses.example: This will give us the tools we need to enforce accounts like these.

senses.definition: To give strength or force to; to affirm, to emphasize.
senses.example: The victim was able to enforce his evidence against the alleged perpetrator.

core.definition: To make people obey a law, rule, or decision, or to make sure something is carried out.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, 'FORS.' The r is clear and rhotic, so don't drop it, and the word has only one main vowel sound after the stress.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, because it suggests authority or compulsion, though it can be positive when rules protect people.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use enforce for laws, policies, and rules, as in 'The police enforce the speed limit,' or 'We need to enforce the new security policy.' In casual speech people may say 'make sure people follow' instead. In workplace talk, enforce often comes up in policy discussions, and it sounds professional.

distinctions.note: Impose means to put a rule or burden on someone; enforce means to make sure the rule is actually followed.
Implement means to put a plan or policy into action; enforce focuses on compliance with a rule.
Reinforce means to strengthen something, often a belief or structure; enforce means to compel obedience.

examples.everyday: My landlord says he will finally enforce the no-pets rule, so my neighbor is worried.
examples.professional: We need to enforce the code review policy before merging to main, or quality will keep slipping.
examples.analytical: A moral community must enforce its norms without destroying the freedom that makes those norms worth keeping.

nuance.analogy: To enforce a rule is like a referee in a game: the rule exists on paper, but the referee makes sure the players actually follow it.
nuance.etymology: From Old French enforcier, from Latin infortiare, 'to strengthen,' from fortis, 'strong.'
common_mistakes: Using enforce with 'of' as in 'enforce of the law'; say 'enforce the law.'
Confusing enforce with force; enforce usually refers to rules and policies, while force is more physical.

enforce.etymology: From Middle English *enforcen*, from Old French *enforcier*, from Late Latin *infortiāre*, from *in-* + *fortis* (“strong”).

senses.definition: A person who sets up a business; generally, a person who owns and manages a business and assumes its financial risks.
(rare) A person who organizes concerts, plays, or other entertainments; the manager of a theater or similar venue; an impresario.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (rare) A person who serves as an intermediary; a middleman; a go-between.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: A person who starts and runs a business, taking on its financial risks in hope of making a profit.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the last syllable, a strong 'ur' sound. The middle syllables are quick and reduced, and the r's are pronounced, unlike in French.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it suggests creativity, initiative, and risk-taking, though it can be used with some irony for overly hyped founders.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use entrepreneur for anyone starting a business, from a food truck owner to a tech founder. It is common in news, business talk, and casual conversation. People may say my cousin is an entrepreneur to mean they run their own company.

distinctions.note: Business owner only means you own a company; entrepreneur implies starting something new and taking on the risk.
Managers run an existing business or team; entrepreneurs usually build the business themselves.

examples.everyday: My cousin is an entrepreneur who opened a bakery downtown last spring.
examples.professional: The startup founder was a classic entrepreneur who handled sales, hiring, and payroll herself.
examples.analytical: In Schumpeter's account, the entrepreneur is the agent whose innovations drive economic change through creative destruction.

nuance.analogy: An entrepreneur is like a pioneer who clears the trail first and carries the risk if the path leads nowhere.
nuance.etymology: From French entreprendre, to undertake.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the last syllable with a French nasal sound instead of a clear American 'ur.'
Misspelling it as entrepeneur, leaving out the r.

entrepreneur.etymology: French *entrepreneur* (“one who undertakes or manages”), from Middle French *entrepreneur*, from *entreprendre* + *-eur*.

senses.definition: Of or relating to epilepsy.
Of or relating to an epileptic or epileptics (epileptic people).
A person who has epilepsy.

core.definition: Relating to epilepsy, a neurological condition marked by recurring seizures. Used in phrases like 'an epileptic seizure.'

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on the third syllable, LEP. Pronounce the middle vowels as quick, reduced sounds, and say the final -tic as 'tik'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in medical contexts, but the noun use can sound outdated or stigmatizing. Americans prefer person-first language.
nuance.usage_note: In American medicine and everyday talk, the adjective is common in phrases like 'epileptic seizure' or 'epileptic disorder.' For people, Americans usually say 'a person with epilepsy' or 'someone who has epilepsy,' because calling someone 'an epileptic' sounds dated and reduces them to the condition. In a medical setting, you may hear 'epileptic patient,' but it is more natural to say 'patient with epilepsy.'

distinctions.note: Epilepsy is the condition itself; epileptic is the adjective describing something related to it.
A seizure is a single episode; epileptic describes a condition or thing linked to epilepsy, not every seizure.

examples.everyday: The doctor ruled out an epileptic cause for her fainting spells, so she didn't need the medication.
examples.professional: The trial enrolled adults with epileptic seizures who had not responded to two prior drugs.
examples.analytical: Matthew describes the boy as epileptic, a diagnosis that shapes how readers understand the healing.

nuance.analogy: Like the word 'cardiac' for the heart: it describes what relates to the condition, not the whole person.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin epilepticus, from Greek epilēptikos, 'seized, attacked,' from epilambanein 'to seize.'
common_mistakes: Calling a person 'an epileptic' in conversation, which many Americans find dated or unkind; say 'a person with epilepsy.'
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in eh-PIL-ep-tik instead of eh-pih-LEP-tik.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Revised Standard Version of Matthew 17:15, a father asks Jesus to heal his son, and the RSV describes the boy as an epileptic. In Greek the text uses selēniazomai, 'to be moonstruck,' a description of seizures. Mark 9:14-29 and Luke 9:37-43 tell the same story, with the boy's fits attributed to a spirit, and Jesus heals him. Modern readers often discuss how ancient language about illness relates to today's medical categories.

senses.definition: In an erratic manner; unsteadily or randomly, unpredictably.
senses.example: When I saw the other driver weaving erratically across the road, I decided to keep my distance.

core.definition: In an unpredictable, inconsistent way; not following a steady or regular pattern.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the syllable RAT. The final '-ically' reduces to 'ik-lee', with the 'ic' sounding like 'ik', not 'ick' as in 'kick' with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral, describing unreliable behavior, movement, or performance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use erratically mostly to describe things that behave unpredictably, such as machines, traffic, or weather. It sounds natural in news and everyday talk about a car, a phone, or a flight. It is less common for describing a person's temper, where 'moody' or 'unpredictable' is more natural.

distinctions.note: Irregularly means without a set pattern or schedule, while erratically suggests changes that are sudden and hard to anticipate.
Unpredictably is a general word for not being foreseeable, while erratically adds a sense of inconsistency or instability.

examples.everyday: The old heater turns on and off erratically, so we're freezing in the mornings.
examples.professional: The API has been responding erratically since last Tuesday, so I'm opening a ticket with the vendor.
examples.analytical: Stock prices moved erratically during the crisis, which made short-term forecasting models unreliable.

nuance.analogy: Something that moves erratically is like a bird flying in zigzags, changing direction without warning.
nuance.etymology: From erratic, from Latin erraticus, meaning wandering, plus the adverb ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as 'erraticaly' instead of 'erratically'.
Stressing the wrong syllable, such as ER-ratically.
Using erratically to describe a person's clear, deliberate choices, where it sounds like criticism.

senses.definition: In terms of experience.

core.definition: In a way based on direct personal experience, or in terms of what is actually lived and felt.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on EN. The final -ly is an unstressed ee sound, and the middle vowel reduces to a short uh sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It highlights personal, first-hand understanding and is used in academic and professional analysis.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use experientially mostly in academic writing, training materials, and careful discussion. In speech they more often say from experience, in practice, or by actually doing it. It is rarely needed in everyday conversation.

distinctions.note: Empirically means by observation or evidence; experientially means through personal, lived involvement.
Practically means in a real-world, useful way; experientially focuses on the process of being through something.

examples.everyday: I understand the hike better now, experientially, since I actually did the whole trail.
examples.professional: We evaluate the prototype experientially by having users complete the task themselves.
examples.analytical: The argument holds experientially, though its metaphysical claim remains untested.

nuance.analogy: Reading a recipe tells you the steps; cooking the dish experientially teaches you how it smells and tastes.
nuance.etymology: From experiential plus the adverb suffix -ly, from Latin experientia.
common_mistakes: Using experientially where from experience or in practice sounds more natural in speech.
Mispronouncing the middle syllables; the stress is on EN, and the vowels around it are reduced.

senses.definition: The design of all information-gathering exercises where variation is present, whether under the full control of the experimenter or not.

core.definition: The plan for collecting data, deciding which units get which treatments, and controlling variation so that results can support valid conclusions.

pronunciation.tip: Main stress falls on MEN in experimental and on ZINE in design. Non-native speakers often over-pronounce the reduced vowels in -al and de-; say them quickly and softly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It signals rigor and methodological care.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use experimental design in statistics, data science, psychology, medicine, and engineering. Data scientists often mean the plan for an A/B test, and the term also covers observational studies where the experimenter does not control the variables. In casual talk, people simply say how the study was set up.

distinctions.note: Study design is a broader term covering observational and experimental studies; experimental design usually implies the researcher manipulates the conditions.
Sampling design concerns how units are selected from a population; experimental design concerns how treatments are assigned and compared.

examples.everyday: My sister is a biologist, and she spent an hour explaining her experimental design to me.
examples.professional: Before we run the A/B test, let's agree on the experimental design and the sample size.
examples.analytical: A rigorous experimental design isolates the treatment effect by randomizing units across conditions, controlling for confounding variables.

nuance.analogy: It is like planning a cooking contest: you decide who cooks what, keep the kitchen conditions fair, and only then taste and compare.
nuance.etymology: Experimental from Latin experimentum, trial; design from Latin designare, to mark out.
common_mistakes: Stressing design on the first syllable; the stress falls on the second syllable, ZINE.
Using experimental design for any study; observational studies without manipulation are not experimental in the strict sense.

senses.definition: Someone who sees an event and can report or testify about it.
To be present at an event or incident, and see and observe it.

core.definition: A person who saw an event happen and can describe it, often as a witness in court or in a report.

pronunciation.tip: Stress EYE, and the final -ness is a weak, reduced syllable close to nuss. The t in the middle is quick, so the word sounds like two syllables plus a light ending.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it signals reliability when the person is credible, but it can be doubted if the account is shaky.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use eyewitness in news reports, police stories, legal settings and everyday talk, as in Were there any eyewitnesses? The verb form appears mostly in writing and reporting. A casual reply might be Oh, I was there, I saw the whole thing.

distinctions.note: Witness is the general word for anyone who sees something and can also mean someone who testifies; eyewitness stresses personally seeing the event.
A bystander is present but may not have been paying attention; an eyewitness observed the event closely enough to describe it.

examples.everyday: My neighbor was walking her dog and was an eyewitness, so she saw the whole thing.
examples.professional: We need an eyewitness account from the technician who was on the floor when the server crashed.
examples.analytical: Eyewitness testimony is valuable yet fallible, since memory reconstructs what was seen rather than replaying it.

nuance.analogy: An eyewitness is like a camera that recorded the scene, though human memory is far less reliable than a camera.
nuance.etymology: From eye plus witness, from Old English witnes (knowledge, testimony).
common_mistakes: Writing eye witness as two words in formal writing; eyewitness is the standard American spelling.
Using eyewitness for anyone who knows about an event; it means someone who saw it directly.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word autoptes means an eyewitness, someone who saw with his own eyes. Luke 1:2 speaks of those who were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word from the beginning. 2 Peter 1:16 says the apostles were eyewitnesses of Christ's majesty, grounding the gospel in what they saw. Acts 1:8 links being witnesses to the power of the Spirit and the mission to the ends of the earth.

senses.definition: To tell invented stories, often those that involve fantasy, such as fables.
A folk story that is not entirely believable.
A folk story that is told for entertainment, and not intended to be taken as true.

core.definition: To tell invented stories, especially fantastic ones, in the manner of fables.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FAB. The middle syllable is quick and reduced, like yuh, so avoid saying a long u sound as in 'fab-you-late.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly playful. It describes creative storytelling rather than deliberate lying.
nuance.usage_note: Fabulate is uncommon in everyday American speech and sounds literary or academic. Americans more often say make up stories or tell tall tales. You might see it in writing about fiction, folklore or a writer who invents fanciful worlds.

distinctions.note: Fabricate implies deliberate deception, while fabulate describes imaginative storytelling without intent to mislead.
Embellish adds decorative details to a real story, while fabulate invents the story itself.
Lie is blunt and everyday, while fabulate is a softer, more literary term.

examples.everyday: My uncle loves to fabulate about his fishing trips, so nobody believes the size of his catch.
examples.professional: In the design review, the product writer began to fabulate scenarios that no user had actually described.
examples.analytical: Early novelists did not merely report events; they fabulated worlds, borrowing the freedom of the fable to examine moral questions.

nuance.analogy: To fabulate is like drawing a map of a country that does not exist, then describing its towns to travelers.
nuance.etymology: From Latin fabulari, 'to talk, tell stories,' from fabula, 'story.'
common_mistakes: Confusing fabulate with fabricate; fabulate has a storytelling sense, while fabricate implies deception.
Using fabulate as a noun for a story; the noun is fabulation.

fabulate.etymology: From Latin *fābulātus*, perfect active participle of *fābulor* (“to tell stories, chat”) (see *-ate*), from *fābula* (“fable”).

senses.definition: The state or condition of being fascinated.
senses.example: To my fascination, the skies turned all kinds of colors.

senses.definition: Something which fascinates.
senses.example: Life after death had always been a great fascination to him.

core.definition: A strong feeling of interest or attraction, or something that holds your attention so completely that you can't look away.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the syllable NAY. The first syllable is a short, reduced vowel, and the -tion ending is pronounced shun, not tee-on.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It describes strong interest, sometimes with a hint of obsession.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fascination in both casual and formal speech to describe a strong interest, as in She has a fascination with old maps. The phrase with fascination is common in writing and storytelling. It can suggest a hint of being overly captivated, so it's not always praise.

distinctions.note: Interest is broad and everyday. Fascination is stronger and suggests the attention is captured more intensely.
Obsession suggests an unhealthy or excessive preoccupation. Fascination is a strong interest without necessarily being unhealthy.

examples.everyday: My dad has a real fascination with old cars, so every weekend we're at some junkyard.
examples.professional: Her fascination with causal inference has pushed the team to rethink how we evaluate experiments.
examples.analytical: Medieval theologians often approached the mystery of the Trinity with a mixture of reverence and intellectual fascination.

nuance.analogy: Fascination is like a tide pulling you toward the shore: you can feel it drawing your attention in, step by step.
nuance.etymology: From Latin fascinatio, enchantment, from fascinare, to bewitch.
common_mistakes: Using fascination as a verb; the verb is fascinate.
Saying fascination for something instead of fascinating; the adjective is fascinating.

fascination.etymology: From Latin fascinare, possibly from Ancient Greek *βασκαίνιεν* (“to speak ill of; to curse”).

senses.definition: On a multilane road, the lane intended or reserved for vehicles overtaking or moving at faster speeds.
Any situation or activity where the pace is very rapid.

core.definition: On a multilane road, the leftmost lane reserved for faster traffic, mainly for passing; also any situation where life or work moves very quickly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LANE, the more prominent word, though both words get some stress. Say it as one smooth phrase, and keep the vowel in fast short and the diphthong in lane clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly positive when describing a busy, exciting life; can suggest risk or burnout when describing a pace that is too intense.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fast lane for the left lane of a highway, which is for passing. Driving in the fast lane when you are not passing is considered rude and is often called 'left-lane hogging.' Figuratively, 'living in the fast lane' describes a glamorous or hectic lifestyle, often with a hint of excess.

distinctions.note: Largely interchangeable in the US for the left lane of a divided highway, though passing lane stresses its function.
Express lane is a lane at a store or toll plaza limited to few items or a fixed route, not a highway lane for speed.

examples.everyday: Move over, buddy, you're sitting in the fast lane and nobody's passing you.
examples.professional: After the merger, our team got into the fast lane and we're shipping features every week now.
examples.analytical: Modern capitalism rewards those who live in the fast lane, which raises questions about whether speed itself has become the measure of success.

nuance.analogy: Like the express track at a train station, where trains pass through without stopping for everyone else.
nuance.etymology: Compound of fast (from Old English fæst, firm) and lane (from Old English lanu, path); the highway sense dates to the twentieth century.
common_mistakes: Saying 'fast line' instead of fast lane.
Using fast lane to mean any quick road rather than the specific passing or high-pace lane.

conversation.text: Don't drive slowly in the fast lane; people will tailgate you.
He flew past us in the fast lane doing at least ninety.
She's been living in the fast lane since she moved to New York.

senses.definition: To cause (a person or animal) to be fat or fatter.
senses.example: We must fatten the turkey in time for Thanksgiving.

senses.definition: To become fat or fatter.
senses.example: He gradually fattened in the five years after getting married.

senses.definition: To make thick or thicker (often something containing paper, especially money).
To become thick or thicker.
To make (soil) fertile and fruitful.
senses.example: to fatten land

senses.definition: To become fertile and fruitful.

core.definition: To make a person or animal fat, or to become fatter; also to make something, such as money, grow larger.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, FAT. The final syllable is a weak, unstressed 'un', often pronounced with a syllabic n.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for animals and food; negative or mildly critical when used about people's bodies.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fatten mostly about farm animals, food preparation and phrasal forms like 'fatten up'. Calling a person 'fattened' is unkind and unusual; people would say 'gain weight' instead. In business talk, people sometimes say that a bonus 'fattens' a bottom line, which is informal.

distinctions.note: Gain weight is the polite, neutral way to talk about people; fatten is mostly used for animals or in the phrase fatten up.
Bulk up means to gain muscle mass, often in exercise or sports; fatten means to add fat.

examples.everyday: My aunt always tries to fatten up the kids with extra pie when they visit.
examples.professional: The vendor's price increase helped fatten the margin, but it hurt our customers.
examples.analytical: The parable's fatted calf is a sign of celebration, yet the story turns on who is invited to share it.

nuance.analogy: To fatten something is like filling a jar to the brim with more of the same stuff until it swells.
nuance.etymology: From fat plus the verb suffix -en, meaning to make or become.
common_mistakes: Using fatten about a person in polite conversation, which can sound rude; use gain weight instead.
Confusing fatten with fasten, which means to attach or secure; the pronunciation and meaning are different.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word sitistos means fattened or fed for feasting, used in the story of the prodigal son. Luke 15:23 describes the father ordering the fatted calf to be brought for a celebration when his son returns. Proverbs 15:17 contrasts a dinner of herbs eaten with love against a fatted ox eaten with hatred, showing that the quality of the relationship matters more than the richness of the food.

senses.definition: The mark or impression left by a foot; a track.
senses.example: The child watched as his footsteps in the sand were washed away by the waves.

senses.definition: The indications or waypoints of a course or direction taken.
senses.example: To walk the footsteps of greatness requires that you start at the bottom of a long stair.

senses.definition: The sound made by walking, running etc.
senses.example: The footsteps of the students echoed in the empty hall.

senses.definition: A step, as in a stair.
senses.example: The garden path had a small footstep down to the main walkway.

senses.definition: The distance between one foot and the next when walking; a pace.
senses.example: Mere footsteps away from the victim lay the murder weapon.

senses.definition: The act of taking a step.
senses.example: Take one more footstep towards me, and I'll make you sorry!

senses.definition: An inclined plane under a hand printing press.

core.definition: The sound made by walking or running, or the marks left by a foot; often used figuratively for someone's path or example.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FUT. The 'ts' cluster in the middle is one sound, so say 'FUT-steps' without an extra vowel between t and s.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It is often used warmly, as in 'follow in someone's footsteps'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'footsteps' for the sound of someone walking ('I heard footsteps upstairs') and for the idiom 'follow in someone's footsteps', meaning to do the same job or take the same path. It is common in everyday speech and writing. A natural reply to a parent's career might be 'You're following in their footsteps, huh?'

distinctions.note: 'Steps' means the act of walking or stairs; 'footsteps' emphasizes the sound or the marks of a person's feet.
'Tracks' are the marks left on the ground, often by an animal or vehicle; 'footsteps' are usually human.

examples.everyday: I heard footsteps on the porch, so I figured it was the neighbor.
examples.professional: Our new hire is following in the footsteps of the team's best data engineer.
examples.analytical: Paul calls on believers to walk in the footsteps of Christ, making the moral example central to discipleship.

nuance.analogy: Footsteps are like a trail of breadcrumbs: they show where someone has been and, for others, where to go next.
nuance.etymology: From 'foot' and 'step', the plural form meaning the sounds or marks made by feet.
common_mistakes: Using 'footsteps' for a single step; 'footstep' is singular.
Saying 'follow the footsteps' without 'in', as in 'follow in her footsteps'.
nuance.biblical_note: In the New Testament, footsteps often describe following Jesus. First Peter 2:21 calls believers to follow in Christ's steps, meaning to imitate his suffering and obedience. Romans 4:12 speaks of walking in the steps of Abraham's faith. The Greek word ichnos, meaning footprint or track, appears in such contexts.

senses.definition: Appearing to be threatening, unfriendly or potentially unpleasant.
The act by which something is forbidden; a prohibition.

core.definition: Looking threatening, stern or unfriendly, so that it seems unpleasant or hard to approach.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, with the first syllable reduced to a schwa. Do not confuse the adjective, pronounced with a short i, with the noun forbidding from forbid, which has the same sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes something that looks dangerous, stern or hostile, such as a place, a face or a manner.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use forbidding to describe places, people or systems that look intimidating, such as a steep mountain or a stern manager. It is more descriptive and somewhat literary than unfriendly. The noun sense, meaning a prohibition, is rare and mostly found in older or legal writing, so do not use it in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: Intimidating describes the effect on a person's confidence, while forbidding describes how something looks or feels, often in a stern or unwelcoming way.
Daunting means a task seems too big to handle; forbidding refers to a threatening or unfriendly appearance or atmosphere.

examples.everyday: That old house on the hill looks kind of forbidding, but the owner is really friendly.
examples.professional: The forbidding interface of the legacy dashboard scares new hires away before they learn the tools.
examples.analytical: Kant's moral law often appears forbidding to those who first encounter its demands, though he saw it as the basis of freedom.

nuance.analogy: Like a tall iron gate with no sign: it does not say no, but it makes you feel you should not walk in.
nuance.etymology: From forbid, from Old English forbeodan, to command against; the adjective developed the sense of threatening appearance in the 1700s.
common_mistakes: Using forbidding to mean forbidden, as in 'a forbidding fruit' instead of 'forbidden fruit'.
Confusing the adjective, which describes appearance, with the rare noun meaning prohibition.

senses.definition: Frenzied and frantic, harried; having extreme enthusiasm or energy.
senses.example: After a week of working at a frenetic pace, she was ready for Saturday.

senses.definition: Characterized by manifestations of delirium or madness.
One who is frenetic.

core.definition: Wildly busy and rushed, full of frantic energy or agitated activity.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, NET. The first syllable is a weak schwa, so do not say it as 'FREE'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or mildly negative. It suggests chaos, stress, or overexcitement rather than calm energy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use frenetic in writing, news, and conversation to describe a hectic pace, such as frenetic trading on Wall Street or a frenetic holiday season. It is a little more formal than busy or crazy, so it fits well in a review or a description. Saying it in casual talk is fine, but it sounds slightly literary.

distinctions.note: Hectic describes a busy schedule or day, while frenetic describes a more agitated, almost frantic energy.
Frantic suggests panic or desperation, while frenetic suggests fast, restless activity.
Frenzied emphasizes a wild loss of control, while frenetic emphasizes constant, high-speed motion.

examples.everyday: The kids were running around the house with frenetic energy before the party started.
examples.professional: The team has been moving at a frenetic pace all week trying to ship the release before Friday.
examples.analytical: Modern journalism often rewards a frenetic rhythm of updates that leaves little room for reflection.

nuance.analogy: A frenetic person is like a bee in a jar, buzzing fast in every direction without getting anywhere calm.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin phreneticus, from Greek phrenitikos, relating to the mind or madness, from phrenitis.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as in 'FRE-netic'; the stress belongs on NET.
Confusing frenetic with frenzy (a noun) and using it as a noun for a state of activity.

frenetic.etymology: From Middle English *frenetik* (also *frentik*, *frentyk*, *frantike* > modern *frantic*), from Old French *frenetike*, from Latin *phreneticus*, from Ancient Greek, from *φρενῖτις* (“delirium”), from *φρήν* (“mind”).

senses.definition: The quality of being generalizable.

core.definition: In data science, the degree to which findings from a sample or model apply to other populations or settings.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on BIL, the syllable before '-ity'. Say 'lye-zuh' quickly, and keep the middle syllables light with reduced vowels.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; it is a positive quality to have in a study.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in research, statistics, and data science reports, especially when discussing whether a study's results hold outside its original sample. In casual talk people would say 'whether it works for other people.' Expect it in methods sections and peer review discussions.

distinctions.note: Validity concerns whether a study measures what it claims; generalizability concerns whether results apply beyond the sample.
Reliability is consistency of measurement; generalizability is the transfer of findings to new contexts.

examples.everyday: My friend asked if the study about sleep applied to older adults, and I said the sample was too small to say.
examples.professional: Before we ship the model, we need to check its generalizability across the three regions.
examples.analytical: External validity and generalizability are often conflated, though a result can be internally valid yet fail to generalize.

nuance.analogy: Generalizability is like a recipe that works in any kitchen, not just the one where it was first tested.
nuance.etymology: From generalize plus -able and -ity, from Latin generalis.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'generality', which is about broadness rather than transfer to new cases.
Placing stress on the wrong syllable, saying 'jen-er-uh-LIZE-uh-bil-ity'.

senses.definition: To cover with a thin layer of gold; to cover with gold leaf.
To adorn.
To decorate with a golden surface appearance.
To give a bright or pleasing aspect to.
To give a brilliant color or flush to one's face; (also) to make appear drunk.

core.definition: To cover a surface with a thin layer of gold, or to make something look more valuable or attractive than it really is.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a short i, like the i in "gift". Make sure the final d is clear and not dropped.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gild mostly in literary writing, art, or the idiom "gild the lily", which means to add unnecessary decoration to something already beautiful. In everyday talk, Americans usually say "gold-plate" or "cover with gold" for the physical sense.

distinctions.note: Plate is a general term for covering metal with a thin layer; gild specifically means covering with gold or gold-like finish.
Embellish means to decorate or add details, which may be true or false; gild implies a surface that makes something look more valuable than it is.

examples.everyday: Don't gild the lily with more frosting, the cake is already perfect.
examples.professional: Our marketing team tends to gild the product description, but customers want clear and honest specs.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that the author gilds the moral failures of the aristocracy, making them appear more elegant than they are.

nuance.analogy: Like brushing a thin layer of gold paint over a plain wooden box so it looks like treasure.
nuance.etymology: From Old English gyldan, from gold.
common_mistakes: Using "guild" for the verb, which is a different word meaning an association.
Using gild as a noun, when the usual noun is gilding or gilt.

gild.etymology: From Middle English *gilden*, *gulden*, from Old English *gyldan* (“to gild, to cover with a thin layer of gold”), from **gulþijan*, from Proto-Germanic **gulþijaną*, from Proto-Germanic **gulþą* (“gold”).

senses.definition: Reflecting with glare.
Blatant, obvious.
senses.example: How could you miss this glaring error? It's right on page one!

senses.definition: Garish.
senses.example: painted in glaring oranges and greens

senses.definition: The act of giving a glare.
(rare) A group of cats.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Very obvious and impossible to ignore, especially a mistake or problem.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable. The r is pronounced, and the second syllable is a short, reduced ih sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it usually describes errors, gaps or problems that should not be overlooked.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use glaring to describe mistakes, omissions and inequalities, as in "a glaring error" or "a glaring omission." It is common in reviews, meetings and news. Calling something glaring is a direct criticism, so use it carefully when talking about a colleague's work.

distinctions.note: Obvious is neutral; glaring adds a sense that the problem is embarrassing or should have been noticed.
Blatant often implies deliberate wrongdoing; glaring describes something very visible, not necessarily intentional.

examples.everyday: The movie had a glaring plot hole that everyone noticed.
examples.professional: The report has a glaring error in the revenue table, so please fix it before we send it out.
examples.analytical: The argument has a glaring gap: it assumes the very conclusion it is trying to prove.

nuance.analogy: Like a bright light shining in your eyes: you cannot miss it.
nuance.etymology: From the verb glare, of uncertain origin, related to bright or dazzling light.
common_mistakes: Using glaring for a positive quality; it usually signals something bad or easy to notice.
Confusing glaring with glare, the noun for bright light; the adjective describes something obvious.

senses.definition: The action or process of graduating and receiving a diploma for completing a course of study (such as from an educational institution).
senses.example: The graduation ball was the students' chance to say goodbye to each other.

senses.definition: A commencement ceremony.
The action or process of leaving a group.
senses.example: graduation from AKB48

senses.definition: A marking (e.g. on a container) indicating a measurement on a scale, usually one of many such markings; the making of such marks.
The exposure of a liquid in large surfaces to the air, so as to hasten its evaporation.
Synonym of gradation.

core.definition: The completion of a course of study, such as high school or college, when a student receives a diploma; also the ceremony where this happens.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the -ay- syllable, so say graj-oo-AY-shun. The -tion ending is pronounced shun, not tee-un.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It celebrates achievement, milestones, and new beginnings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'graduation' constantly for high school, college, and graduate programs. Friends and family often attend, and the ceremony is called a commencement at colleges, while high schools often say graduation. A natural reply to someone announcing it is 'Congratulations!' or 'Congrats, what's next for you?'

distinctions.note: Commencement is the formal ceremony at a college or university, while graduation is the broader act of completing a program and receiving the diploma.
A dropout leaves school without finishing, the opposite of completing a program through graduation.

examples.everyday: Graduation is next Saturday, so we're having a barbecue in the backyard after the ceremony.
examples.professional: Her graduation from the data science program is in June, and she has already started applying for jobs.
examples.analytical: Graduation from a doctoral program marks a shift from being trained within a discipline to being held accountable for producing original knowledge.

nuance.analogy: Graduation is like crossing a finish line that also opens a new road.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin graduatio, from Latin gradus, step, in the sense of academic degree.
common_mistakes: Using 'graduated in' where Americans say 'graduated from' a school or program.
Confusing the noun graduation with the verb graduate, which has no -ion ending.

conversation.text: My daughter's graduation is in June.
What are you getting him for graduation?
We're having a graduation party in the backyard.

senses.definition: Irritable; easily upset; angry; tending to complain.
senses.example: His boss gets grouchy when deadlines draw near.

core.definition: Irritable, easily annoyed, and likely to complain or speak sharply when tired or unhappy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, GROUCH. The ch is pronounced like the ch in church, and the final vowel is a light ee.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative and informal. It is used affectionately for people who are temporarily cranky, such as after a late night.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say grouchy about someone who is in a bad mood, often because they are tired or hungry. It is friendly and common in family and workplace talk, but it can sound childish if used for a serious anger problem. Stronger words include hostile or furious.

distinctions.note: Irritable is slightly more formal and can describe a medical or lasting condition, while grouchy is casual and temporary.
Angry describes a stronger emotion, while grouchy describes a mood of complaining and irritation.

examples.everyday: Don't mind Dad, he's grouchy because he skipped lunch.
examples.professional: The team got grouchy during the long review, so we took a short break.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that grouchy complaint can sometimes hide a deeper moral seriousness.

nuance.analogy: Like a bear that wakes up too early, grumbling at everything it sees.
nuance.etymology: From grouch, meaning to grumble, probably from Middle English grucchen.
common_mistakes: Using grouchy for serious anger; it is mild and informal.
Pronouncing the ch as k or sh instead of the ch in church.

senses.definition: A customary way of speaking or acting; a fashion, a manner, a practice (often used formerly in such phrases as "at his own guise"; that is, in his own fashion, to suit himself.)
An external appearance in manner or dress; an appropriate indication or expression; a garb; a shape.
A misleading appearance; a cover, a cloak.
senses.example: Under the guise of patriotism

senses.definition: Deliberate misspelling of guys.
senses.example: Sup guise? — What's up, guys?

core.definition: An outward appearance or form, often one that hides what something really is; a false or misleading front.

pronunciation.tip: One syllable with a long i sound, like 'guy' plus a z at the end. The word is often misspelled as 'guize' or 'guyse', so remember it is spelled g-u-i-s-e.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It is neutral when describing an appearance, but it often suggests deception when used with 'under the guise of'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use guise mostly in writing, news reports, and careful speech, usually in the phrases 'under the guise of' and 'in the guise of'. In casual talk people say 'pretending to be' or 'posing as' instead. Older senses about fashion or manner are rare today and not needed for everyday use.

distinctions.note: Disguise is the more common everyday word for hiding one's identity with costume or appearance, and it can be a verb. Guise is a noun and is more formal and abstract.
Pretense focuses on a false claim or act of pretending, while guise focuses on the outward form that presents the false impression.

collocations: in the guise of a charity

examples.everyday: He said he was just stopping by to say hi, but he was really there to borrow money under the guise of a friendly visit.
examples.professional: The vendor pitched the upgrade under the guise of a routine security patch, which made it hard to tell what it actually changed.
examples.analytical: Propaganda often works by presenting partisan claims in the guise of neutral information, so the audience never sees the argument as argument.

nuance.analogy: A guise is like a costume that looks so real people forget there is someone underneath.
nuance.etymology: From Old French 'guise', meaning manner or way, from a Germanic root related to 'wise' in the sense of way or manner.
common_mistakes: Using 'guise' as a verb; it is only a noun, so say 'disguise' for the verb.
Writing 'in the guise to' instead of 'in the guise of'.

guise.etymology: From Middle English *guise*, *gise*, *gyse*, from Old French *guisse*, *guise*, *vise* (“guise, manner, way”), from Old **wīsā* (“manner, way, fashion”), from Proto-Germanic **wīsǭ* (“manner, way”), from Proto-Indo-European **weyd-* (“to see, view, behold,…

senses.definition: The halftime show, the primary light entertainment of a game, after the second quarter, when players can physically recover, coaches can give players a pep talk, bets can be doubled, etc.

core.definition: The break between the two halves of a game, especially American football or basketball, when teams rest and adjust.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the 'half' vowel short, like 'hat'. The second syllable 'time' is a clear diphthong, and the word is one compound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and everyday in sports talk; it can also be used to mean a halfway point of any event.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use halftime for the break in the middle of a football, basketball or soccer game, with 'the halftime show' being the entertainment during the Super Bowl. In soccer and many other sports Americans still say halftime. You might say 'We're up by seven at halftime' during a game with friends.

distinctions.note: Intermission is the break in a play, concert or movie; halftime is for sports games.
A timeout is a short stoppage called during a half, often by a coach; halftime is the longer break between halves.

examples.everyday: Let's grab a snack at halftime so we don't miss the start of the second half.
examples.professional: Our marketing team will review the campaign numbers at halftime of the quarterly meeting.
examples.analytical: The coach's halftime adjustments shifted the team's defense, which shows how much a short break can change the course of a game.

nuance.analogy: Like a pause at the middle of a long movie, when you refill your drink and talk about what has happened so far.
nuance.etymology: From 'half' (Old English healf) and 'time'; the sports sense developed in the nineteenth century.
common_mistakes: Saying 'half time' as two words in formal writing; American usage is usually one word.
Using halftime for any break in a non-sports event; intermission is the better word.

conversation.text: The score was tied at halftime.
Let's grab food during halftime so we don't miss anything.
Who's doing the halftime show this year?

senses.definition: To pass (the ball) to a teammate.
To pass or transfer.
senses.example: Before we hand off the project to him, let's make sure to write some instructions.

core.definition: To pass a task, responsibility or object to another person or team, often in a planned transfer.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'off', and in General American the vowel in 'off' is the same as in 'cot' and 'caught', so say 'AWF' with an open, rounded vowel. Do not stress 'hand' as much as 'off'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly informal. In work settings it can sound efficient, but it can also imply that someone is dumping a task.
nuance.usage_note: In American workplaces, 'hand off' is common for passing a project to a colleague: 'I'll hand off the dashboard to Sam next week.' In sports it refers to passing the ball, especially in football and basketball. A natural reply is 'Sounds good, I'll pick it up from there.'

distinctions.note: 'Hand off' often suggests a quick, informal transfer of a task or object; 'hand over' suggests a formal transfer of control or authority.
'Delegate' is a management term that implies assigning work while the manager keeps overall responsibility; 'hand off' can mean a complete transfer.
'Pass on' can mean transfer or forward information; 'hand off' more often refers to a concrete task or object.

collocations: hand off to the next team

examples.everyday: I have to leave early, so can you hand off the dishes to Jake when he gets home?
examples.professional: We'll hand off the migration work to the platform team once the testing is finished.
examples.analytical: In a handoff between two research teams, the risk is that tacit knowledge is lost along with the formal documentation.

nuance.analogy: Like a relay runner passing the baton: the race continues, but the responsibility moves to the next runner.
nuance.etymology: From 'hand' plus 'off', from Old English 'hand' and 'of'.
common_mistakes: Using 'hand off' as a noun with a hyphen in formal writing when 'handoff' is more common.
Confusing it with 'hand out', which means to distribute.

conversation.text: I'll hand off the project to Lisa when I go on leave.
Let's plan how you'll hand off your work before you change teams.
Mike handed off the client to the new account manager.

senses.definition: Work done by the hands.
A handmade object; a handicraft.
senses.example: The Museum of Popular Arts showcases Portugal's finest handiworks.

senses.definition: Work done personally.
senses.example: The street names are the handiwork of city planners.

senses.definition: The result of personal efforts.

core.definition: Something made or done by a person's own hands or effort, often used for a result that shows a person's skill.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, 'HAN'. The second syllable is a light 'dee', and the final syllable has an American r-colored vowel, so say 'wurk' rather than 'wok'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests skill, care and personal effort, and it is often used with mild praise or irony.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'handiwork' for crafts, sewing, woodworking or someone's personal results: 'This quilt is her handiwork.' It can also be used ironically for a mess someone caused: 'Look at this traffic jam, the mayor's handiwork.' In casual talk, 'handmade' or 'homemade' is more common for objects.

distinctions.note: 'Handicraft' usually refers to a craft or type of art; 'handiwork' can refer to a specific object or to someone's results more broadly.
'Workmanship' refers to the quality of making something; 'handiwork' refers to the thing made, or the person who made it.
'Creation' can refer to anything made, including ideas; 'handiwork' is more concrete and personal.

examples.everyday: Look at this bookshelf my dad built, it's all his handiwork.
examples.professional: The clean API design is clearly the handiwork of the senior engineer who wrote the original service.
examples.analytical: In Psalm 19, the created order is read as God's handiwork, and that reading shapes how creation is understood as revelation.

nuance.analogy: Like a signature in a painting: the work carries the mark of the person who made it.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'hand' and 'weorc', meaning hand-work.
common_mistakes: Using 'handiwork' as a plural noun, as in 'handiworks'.
Using it as a verb or adjective, which is not standard.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, handiwork refers to what God has made, especially the created world, and in some passages to a person's deeds. The Hebrew behind it is ma'aseh (מַעֲשֶׂה), meaning work or deed, and the Greek ergon, meaning work. Psalm 19:1 (RSV) says the firmament proclaims God's handiwork, showing creation as a testimony to God's power and wisdom. Psalm 8:6 (RSV) speaks of humanity having dominion over the works of God's hands, which is closely related. Ephesians 2:10 (RSV) calls believers God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which connects the idea of God's making with human vocation.

handiwork.etymology: From Middle English *hondywerk*, *handiwerc*, from Old English *handġeweorc* (“work done by hand, creation”), from *hand* (“hand”) + *ġeweorc* (“work”).

core.definition: An Israelite leader after the exile, a descendant of David's line who helped rebuild Jerusalem and took part in the covenant renewal.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, make the vowel in the second syllable a short 'uh,' and end on a clear 'sh.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a biblical proper name.
nuance.usage_note: Americans encounter Hattush in Bible study, especially when reading Ezra and Nehemiah. It is not used outside religious or historical contexts. Good to recall when discussing the rebuilding of the wall.

distinctions.note: Hattush is a named leader with an active role in Ezra and Nehemiah, while Hattaavah appears only in a list of returnees.

examples.everyday: In our Bible study, we talked about Hattush, one of the leaders who came back from exile with Ezra.
examples.professional: In my lesson on Nehemiah, I pointed out that Hattush rebuilt a section of the wall opposite his own house.
examples.analytical: Hattush's presence in the lists of Ezra and Nehemiah shows how the restored community linked its leaders to the Davidic line.

nuance.analogy: Hattush is like a foreman on a rebuilding crew who fixes the section of wall nearest his own home.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.
Confusing Hattush with Hathach, the eunuch in Esther.
nuance.biblical_note: Hattush appears in Ezra 8:2, where he returns with Ezra from Babylon as a head of a family, and in Nehemiah 3:10, where he repairs the wall opposite his house. Nehemiah 10:4 lists him among those who sealed the covenant, showing his role in the community's renewal.

senses.definition: With the head first or down.
With an unrestrained forward motion.
senses.example: Figures out today show the economy plunging headlong into recession.

senses.definition: Rashly; precipitately; without deliberation; in haste, hastily.
Precipitous.
Plunging downwards head foremost.
Rushing forward without restraint.
Reckless; impetuous.
To precipitate.

core.definition: Moving forward quickly and without caution, thought, or hesitation; or falling head first.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, HED. The second syllable is the vowel in law followed by ng; Americans with the cot-caught merger often pronounce it with a broad o sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It suggests recklessness or haste.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use headlong mainly in writing or formal speech to describe rushing into something without thinking. It is rarely used in casual conversation. Americans would more likely say rushing into something or without thinking in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: Headfirst is the common everyday word for going head first, while headlong has a stronger sense of speed and haste.
Hastily simply means quickly; headlong suggests a reckless, unthinking rush.

examples.everyday: Don't rush headlong into buying a car without checking the price first.
examples.professional: The team rushed headlong into the product launch without validating the data, and the bugs appeared within a week.
examples.analytical: Rushing headlong into moral conclusions before analyzing the evidence can mislead even careful thinkers.

nuance.analogy: Headlong is like a skier who points downhill and goes straight, without turning or slowing down.
nuance.etymology: From head plus long, from an older sense of plunging head first, later extended to rushing without thought.
common_mistakes: Using headlong to mean simply head first in everyday talk; headfirst is more natural.
Confusing headlong with headstrong, which describes a stubborn personality.

headlong.etymology: From Middle English *hedlong*, alteration of *hedling*, *heedling*, *hevedlynge* (“headlong”), assimilated to *long*.

senses.definition: A place or situation of great suffering in life.
senses.example: My new boss is making my job a hell.

senses.definition: A place for gambling.
An extremely hot place.
senses.example: You don’t have a snowball's chance in hell.

senses.definition: Used as an intensifier in phrases grammatically requiring a noun.
senses.example: I’m as mad as hell and I’m not going to take it anymore.

senses.definition: In certain games of chase, a place to which those who are caught are carried for detention.
Something extremely painful or harmful (to)
senses.example: That steep staircase is hell on my knees.

senses.definition: Used to express discontent, unhappiness, or anger.
senses.example: Oh, hell! I got another parking ticket.

senses.definition: Used to emphasize.
senses.example: Hell yeah!

senses.definition: Used to introduce an intensified statement following an understated one; nay; not only that, but.
senses.example: Do it, or, rest assured, there will be no more Middle Eastern crisis – hell, there will be no more Middle East!

senses.definition: Very; used to emphasize strongly.
senses.example: That was hell good!

senses.definition: To make hellish; to place (someone) in hell; to make (a place) into a hell.
To hurry, rush.
To move quickly and loudly; to raise hell as part of motion.
senses.example: He was helling down the road with his radio blaring.

senses.definition: (rare) To add luster to; to burnish (silver or gold).
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (rare) To pour.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: In Christianity, the place or state of punishment and separation from God after death; also, a situation of great suffering.

pronunciation.tip: One syllable with a short 'e' as in 'bed'. Pronounce the final 'l' with the tongue tip touching behind the upper teeth; do not drop it or add a vowel.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. Religious use is solemn; as an expletive it is mildly profane.
nuance.usage_note: In religious contexts it is a normal term. As a swear word ('What the hell?', 'hell yeah') it is common but impolite in formal settings, at work with strangers or around children. 'Hell of a' is informal and can be positive ('a hell of a game'). Avoid it in professional writing unless discussing theology.

distinctions.note: The Greek realm of the dead, not necessarily a place of punishment.
The Hebrew Bible's realm of the dead, without a clear division between punishment and reward.
The New Testament Greek name for the place of fiery judgment, often translated 'hell'.
A stronger verb or interjection of cursing; 'hell' names the place.

examples.everyday: What the hell happened to the highway? It took us three hours to go ten miles.
examples.professional: That migration was hell, but the new system is finally stable.
examples.analytical: Whether hell is eternal conscious torment, annihilation, or the final possibility of self-chosen exclusion remains disputed among Christian theologians.

nuance.analogy: For many believers, a place of separation like a locked door from the source of all life.
nuance.etymology: Old English 'hel', from Proto-Germanic *haljō, 'the concealed place', related to 'hide'.
common_mistakes: Using it casually in formal settings; it can seem rude.
Mispronouncing it as 'heel' or adding a vowel after 'l'.
Assuming every Bible mention of 'hell' translates the same word: Sheol, Hades and Gehenna differ.
nuance.biblical_note: The RSV uses 'hell' mainly for Greek 'Gehenna' (from Hebrew 'Ge Hinnom', the Valley of Hinnom), as in Matthew 5:22 and Mark 9:43-48, where Jesus warns of fiery judgment. Matthew 10:28 speaks of God's power to destroy soul and body in hell. In Revelation 20:14-15, death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire. The RSV often leaves 'Sheol' and 'Hades' untranslated.

traditions.view: Hell is often understood as the experience of God's uncreated love and light by those who reject him, not a separate torture chamber. Many Orthodox writers stress that the final outcome rests in God's mercy and do not formally teach universal salvation.

Hell is the state of definitive self-exclusion from communion with God, resulting from unrepented mortal sin. The Church teaches it is eternal, and does not declare that any particular person is there.
Most Protestants affirm hell as real, conscious and eternal punishment for the unrepentant. Some evangelicals, including some Anglicans, hold annihilationism, and a few hold hopeful universalism.

hell.etymology: From Middle English *hel*, *hell*, *helle*, *hælle*, from Old English *hel*, *hell*, from **hallju*, from Proto-Germanic **haljō* (“hell, netherworld”), from Proto-Indo-European **ḱel-* (“to cover”).

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to herbs.
Full of herbal aroma or flavor.

core.definition: Tasting or smelling strongly of herbs, or made with a lot of herbs.

pronunciation.tip: The h is silent. Stress the first syllable, and end with a clear ee sound, not ih.

nuance.connotation: Positive when describing food; it sounds casual and cozy.
nuance.usage_note: Herby is informal and is used mostly in everyday talk about cooking, as in This sauce is really herby. Menus and cookbooks often prefer herb-flavored or herbal. Herbal usually describes teas and medicines, not the taste of food.

distinctions.note: Herbal often refers to teas or remedies, while herby describes the flavor or smell of food.

examples.everyday: This chicken is so herby and fresh, I want seconds.
examples.professional: The new pesto is herby but not too strong, so it should work for the lunch menu.
examples.analytical: The herby quality of the sauce comes from fresh basil and parsley rather than from dried spices.

nuance.analogy: Herby is to food what grassy is to a lawn: the green scent is the first thing you notice.
nuance.etymology: Formed from herb with the adjective suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Using herby for medicinal plants, where herbal is the better word
Pronouncing the h

conversation.text: The potatoes are herby and buttery.
I made an herby sauce with parsley and basil.
The salad was fresh and herby.

core.definition: In the Bible, a son of Canaan and the ancestor of the Hittites, the people from whom Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce it as one syllable with a voiceless th at the end, like the th in 'math'. Do not add a vowel after the th.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a name from the Bible with no positive or negative charge.
nuance.usage_note: Heth is used almost only in Bible study, sermons, and discussions of Genesis. Americans who read the Bible will recognize it immediately. In casual talk you would only mention it while discussing the Bible or Hittite history.

distinctions.note: Heth is the name of the ancestor (or the ancestral family line) in Genesis, while Hittite is the usual name for the people and the later Anatolian kingdom.

examples.everyday: My Bible study group is reading about Abraham buying a burial plot from the sons of Heth.
examples.professional: In the Genesis lesson I'm teaching, I'll point out that the sons of Heth are the Hittites who sold Abraham the field at Machpelah.
examples.analytical: The phrase sons of Heth in Genesis 23 functions as an ethnic designation, and the text presents Abraham as a resident alien negotiating with them as equals.

nuance.analogy: Heth is like a family name at the top of a family tree: everyone called a 'Heth' descends from him, just as the Hittites were remembered as his descendants.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Ḥēṯ; the meaning of the name is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Saying it with a long e, as in 'heeth'; the vowel is short, as in 'bet'.
Confusing Heth with Hess or Hesh, which are different names.
nuance.biblical_note: Heth (Hebrew Ḥēṯ) is named as the son of Canaan in the Table of Nations, and his descendants are called the sons of Heth, or Hittites. Genesis 10:15 lists Heth among Canaan's sons, placing the Hittites among the peoples of Canaan. Genesis 23:3-20 tells how Abraham bargained with the sons of Heth, including Ephron the Hittite, to buy the cave of Machpelah as a burial place for Sarah. Genesis 27:46 has Rebekah complain about Esau's Hittite wives, the daughters of Heth, which shows the family's concern about marrying within their own people.

senses.definition: A success, especially a popular success.
senses.example: The product was a home run.

senses.definition: A three-base hit, a legal hit where the batter gets to third base without stopping illegally and without the opposing team attempting to put the batter out on earlier bases, scoring one run immediately.
The portion of a journey that ends at home.
senses.example: I'm on the home run.

senses.definition: Sexual intercourse.
A connection from a central distribution point or circuit breaker to a destination.
A four-base hit, allowing the batter to circle the bases and reach home safely in one play without any errors being committed by the defensive team.
senses.example: The first baseman hit a home run to lead off the ninth.

core.definition: In baseball, a hit that lets the batter run around all the bases and score. Also used figuratively for a great success.

pronunciation.tip: Stress 'home' as the main beat and 'run' as a lighter secondary stress. The 'r' is pronounced, and the vowel in 'run' is the short 'uh' sound, not 'oo'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it signals a strong success, especially when used figuratively.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'home run' most often in baseball, but also in everyday speech for a major success, as in 'hit a home run.' It is casual and widely understood. You might say 'That was a home run!' and a natural reply is 'Thanks, we worked hard on it.'

distinctions.note: A grand slam is a home run hit with the bases loaded, which scores four runs; a home run may score one to four runs.
A homer is informal American slang for a home run, common in sports broadcasting and conversation.

collocations: a home run for the team
a home run for our business
a home run with the client
hit it out of the park

examples.everyday: Your pie was a home run at the cookout; everyone asked for the recipe.
examples.professional: The new onboarding flow was a home run with customers, and the support tickets dropped by a third.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the policy was not a home run but a partial success, since its benefits were concentrated among a small group of users.

nuance.analogy: Like a batter who hits the ball over the fence: one clean swing, and everyone on the team scores.
nuance.etymology: 'Home' from Old English ham; 'run' from Old English rinnan, 'to flow or run'; the baseball term dates to the late 19th century.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'run' as 'roon', with a long vowel.
Saying 'homerun' as one word in formal writing; the standard is two words or a hyphen when used as an adjective.

conversation.text: He hit a home run in his first at-bat.
That ball is going, going... it's a home run!
Your presentation was a home run; everyone loved it.

senses.definition: In a hubristic manner; with hubris.

core.definition: In an excessively proud or overconfident way, often in a manner that invites failure or criticism.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress shifts from HYOO in the adjective to STIK in the adverb, and the final syllable is 'lee,' not 'lik.'

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies overconfidence that deserves criticism or may lead to failure.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'hubristically' in essays, political commentary, criticism and formal discussion. It is rare in everyday conversation. Casual speakers would say 'way too confidently' or 'with way too much swagger.'

distinctions.note: 'Arrogantly' describes an attitude; 'hubristically' suggests an overreaching action that is likely to end badly.
'Confidently' is neutral or positive; 'hubristically' is critical and implies excessive pride.

examples.professional: The team hubristically assumed the old pipeline would scale without changes, and that is why the outage happened.
examples.analytical: The historian argues that the empire acted hubristically, confident that its power would last forever.

nuance.analogy: Like a runner who sprints the first mile at full speed, sure he can keep it up: the overconfidence sets up the collapse.
nuance.etymology: Formed from hubristic with the adverb suffix -ally.
common_mistakes: Moving the stress to the wrong syllable, as in 'hyoo-BRIS-tik-lee.'
Using it as a neutral word for confidence; it carries criticism.

senses.definition: Containing perceptible moisture (usually describing air or atmosphere); damp; moist; somewhat wet or watery.
senses.example: humid earth

core.definition: Containing a lot of moisture in the air, making the weather feel damp and warm.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. Many Americans begin with a yod, so the word sounds like 'HYOO-mid', and the last syllable is short, not 'meed'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It describes uncomfortable weather, though it can be neutral in a weather report.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use humid constantly in weather talk, especially in summer in the South, the Midwest, and along the East Coast. It is neutral and polite, and it is the normal word for describing sticky air. A typical phrase is 'It's so humid today,' and a natural reply is 'I know, I can barely breathe.'

distinctions.note: Muggy is a more informal everyday word for warm, humid, and uncomfortable weather, often used in conversation.
Damp describes something slightly wet, like a towel or a basement, while humid describes the moisture in the air.

examples.everyday: It's so humid outside that my hair is frizzing already.
examples.professional: The server room can run warm, but the humidity sensors show the air stays within range.
examples.analytical: A humid climate shapes the agricultural calendar and the cultural rhythms of daily life.

nuance.analogy: Humid air is like a wet sponge that is still dry to the touch: the moisture is there, but you feel it on your skin.
nuance.etymology: From Latin humidus, meaning moist, from humere, to be moist.
common_mistakes: Saying 'humidity' when you mean the adjective: say 'It's humid,' not 'It's humidity.'
Pronouncing it as 'HOO-mid' with no yod sound.

humid.etymology: Borrowed from Old French *humide*, from Latin *humidus* (“moist”).

conversation.text: It's really humid in Florida in the summer.
My hair goes crazy when it's humid.
It's so humid that my glasses fog up when I step outside.

senses.definition: One of a race of people living in the extreme north, beyond the north wind.
senses.example: The Hyperboreans venerated Apollo over the other gods.

senses.definition: Any person living in a northern country, or to the north.
Pertaining to the extreme north of the earth; or to a specific northern country or area.

core.definition: Of the far northern regions of the earth, extremely cold and remote, beyond the north wind.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the third syllable, -BOR-. The middle 'ee' is a long vowel, and the ending is 'in', not 'an'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to literary. It evokes a remote, very cold, mythic north.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use hyperborean in conversation. It appears in poetry, fantasy writing, and classical studies, usually to describe an imagined far north. In modern speech, people say 'northern' or 'arctic' instead.

distinctions.note: Arctic is the everyday, precise word for the far north, while hyperborean is literary and often mythic.
Northern is neutral and common, while hyperborean suggests a remote, legendary land.

examples.professional: The hyperborean conditions described in the report made the field operation sound brutal and unrealistic.
examples.analytical: The Greeks imagined a hyperborean land of perpetual blessing beyond the north wind, which shows their sense of the far edge of the known world.

nuance.analogy: A hyperborean land is like the blank northern edge on an old map, a place that feels both real and mythical.
nuance.etymology: From Greek hyperboreios, 'beyond the north wind', from hyper, 'beyond', and Boreas, 'the north wind'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'HY-per-bor-ee-an'.
Using hyperborean as a general word for any cold place, when it sounds literary and mythic.

hyperborean.etymology: From Late Latin *hyperboreanus*, cognate with Classical Latin *hyperboreus*, from Ancient Greek *ὑπερβόρεος*, composed of *ὑπέρ* (“over”) + *βόρειος* (“northern”).

senses.definition: A level of veneration higher than dulia but less than latria, properly given to the Virgin Mary only.

core.definition: In Catholic theology, the special veneration given to the Virgin Mary, higher than that given to other saints but below worship due to God.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LY, the fourth syllable, which sounds like 'eye'. The first syllable 'hy' also sounds like 'high' with secondary stress.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; technical term in Catholic doctrine, disputed by many Protestants.
nuance.usage_note: A specialist term in Catholic theology and apologetics, rarely heard outside seminaries or debates over Marian devotion. It belongs to a three-part scheme: latria, hyperdulia, dulia.

distinctions.note: Dulia is the veneration given to saints and angels; hyperdulia is the higher honor reserved for Mary.
Latria is worship due to God alone; hyperdulia is not worship.
Veneration is the general word; hyperdulia is its specific Marian degree.

examples.professional: In the theology seminar, we defined hyperdulia as the special honor owed to Mary as Mother of God.
examples.analytical: Aquinas's distinction between latria, dulia and hyperdulia lets Catholics defend Marian devotion against the charge of idolatry.

nuance.analogy: On a ladder of honor, dulia is a step for the saints, hyperdulia is a higher step for Mary, and latria alone belongs to God.
nuance.etymology: Medieval Latin from Greek hyper, 'above', and douleia, 'servitude, service'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable instead of LY.
Confusing it with latria (worship of God).
Calling it 'worship of Mary'.
nuance.biblical_note: The category itself is not in Scripture, but Catholics point to Luke 1:28 and Luke 1:48, where Gabriel greets Mary as favored and Mary says all generations will call her blessed. Elizabeth's greeting in Luke 1:42-43 also honors her as mother of the Lord.

traditions.view: Hyperdulia is the highest level of veneration, given to Mary as Mother of God, always distinct from latria, which is due to God alone.
Orthodoxy honors Mary as Theotokos and 'more honorable than the cherubim', and distinguishes veneration from worship, though it does not usually use the Latin term hyperdulia.
Most Protestants reject the category and are wary of Marian devotion as lacking biblical warrant. Lutherans and Anglicans honor Mary more readily than Baptists or Reformed groups do.

hyperdulia.etymology: From Medieval Latin *hyperdūlīa*, from *hyper-*, from Ancient Greek *ὑπέρ* (“above”) + *dūlīa*, from Ancient Greek *δουλείᾱ* (“slavery”), from *δοῦλος* (“slave”).

senses.definition: The side of a right triangle opposite the right angle.

core.definition: The longest side of a right triangle, which is opposite the right angle.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, PAH. The middle syllables are weak, so the word is not hy-pot-EN-use; the t is a clear t, not a flap.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, a standard school and technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Every American learns this word in middle school geometry, so it comes up in homework help, engineering and construction. People often say 'the long side' in casual talk, but 'hypotenuse' is the expected term in any math setting. Remember that it is always the side opposite the right angle.

distinctions.note: A leg is one of the two shorter sides that form the right angle; the hypotenuse is the side opposite it and is always longest.
A diagonal is a line joining non-adjacent corners of a polygon; in a right triangle the hypotenuse is a side, not a diagonal.

examples.everyday: My son was struggling with his homework, so I reminded him that the hypotenuse is always the longest side of a right triangle.
examples.professional: The contractor measured the hypotenuse of the roof brace to confirm that the rafters were cut to the right length.
examples.analytical: By the Pythagorean theorem, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the two legs, which is why the relation holds only for right triangles.

nuance.analogy: Think of the hypotenuse as the ramp that spans from the bottom of a wall to the top of a step, cutting across the corner.
nuance.etymology: From Latin hypotenusa, from Greek hypoteinousa, meaning stretching under, from hypo- under and teinein to stretch.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing it with the stress on the wrong syllable, such as hy-POT-en-use.
Thinking any long side of a triangle is the hypotenuse; it applies only to the side opposite the right angle in a right triangle.

hypotenuse.etymology: From Latin *hypotenusa*, from Ancient Greek *ὑποτείνουσα πλευρά* (“side subtending [the right angle]”), from *ὑποτείνουσα* (“stretching, extending, subtending”), active participle of *ὑποτείνω* (“subtend, stretch under”).

senses.definition: Impervious to limitation, without limit.
