senses.definition: To start or enable a device by turning a switch or a lever.
To change one's expression or appearance as if by turning a switch.
To arouse, to excite (sexually).

core.definition: To start a device or light working by turning its switch or button to the on position.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the particle 'on' with a broad vowel close to 'ahn.' Keep the 'sw' cluster together, and don't insert an extra vowel after 'switch.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical; it is used in everyday instructions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'Switch on the lamp' or 'Did you switch on the dishwasher?' at home or work. In everyday speech, 'turn on' is just as common and sounds a little more natural. The sense of changing your mood or manner ('switch on the charm') is informal and figurative.

distinctions.note: Almost the same in meaning; 'turn on' is the more common everyday phrase in American speech.
'Power on' is used for computers and electronics and sounds more technical.

examples.everyday: Can you switch on the porch light? It's getting dark out here.
examples.professional: Switch on the new firewall rule before the audit starts tomorrow morning.
examples.analytical: The theory assumes that the brain's reward circuitry can be switched on by a single kind of stimulus, a claim the experiments do not support.

nuance.analogy: Like a light switch that changes the room from dark to bright in an instant.
nuance.etymology: 'Switch' comes from a Middle English word for a thin flexible rod; 'on' is from Old English.
common_mistakes: Using 'switch on' for people, as in 'He switched on early,' which is unnatural; use 'wake up' or 'get going.'
Confusing it with 'switch to,' which means changing from one thing to another.

conversation.text: Can you switch on the air conditioning? It's hot in here.
He switched the TV on to watch the game.

senses.definition: A casual goodbye on the phone.

core.definition: A casual American way to say goodbye, especially at the end of a phone call, meaning we will speak again soon.

pronunciation.tip: In fast speech 'to you' sounds like 'tuh-yoo' or 'chu', and 'later' has a flapped 't' that sounds like a soft 'd'. Stress 'LAY' strongly.

nuance.connotation: Friendly and relaxed; it closes a conversation warmly without formality.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this to friends, family, and coworkers at the end of calls or chats. It can be shortened to 'Talk later' or 'Later!' among close friends. A natural reply is 'Okay, talk to you later!' or 'Bye!'. In a formal or customer-service call, people usually say 'Thank you for calling' instead.

distinctions.note: 'Talk to you later' is slightly more casual and does not specify when; 'talk soon' suggests the next call will be sooner.
'Goodbye' ends the conversation without expecting a future call, while this phrase signals that more contact will follow.

collocations: OK, talk to you later, bye

examples.everyday: Okay, I have to go pick up the kids. Talk to you later!
examples.professional: I need to jump into another meeting, so let's wrap up. Talk to you later this afternoon.
examples.analytical: The phrase 'talk to you later' signals social closure while keeping the relationship open, a small but telling ritual of American politeness.

nuance.analogy: Like closing a door gently while leaving it slightly ajar.
nuance.etymology: Built from 'talk' (Old English tala), 'to', 'you', and 'later' (Old English laetra, meaning slower or more delayed).
common_mistakes: Saying 'Talk you later' without 'to', which sounds unfinished.
Pronouncing 'later' with a crisp 't' instead of the American flap.

conversation.text: OK, talk to you later! Say hi to Mom.
I've got to run. Talk to you later.
"See you Friday?" "Yep. Talk to you later."

senses.definition: A percussion instrument consisting of a small, usually wooden, hoop closed on one side with a drum frame and featuring jingling metal disks on the tread; it is most often held in the hand and shaken rhythmically; by extension, any frame drum.
A tambourine dove (Turtur tympanistria).
A kind of Provençal dance.
The music for this dance.
To play the tambourine.
To make a sound like a tambourine.

core.definition: A small hand-held percussion instrument: a wooden or plastic hoop with metal jingles set into its rim, shaken or struck with the hand.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the last syllable, 'reen'. Keep the middle syllable very short, and do not pronounce an 'o' sound in the second syllable as in 'tom-bo-reen'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and cheerful; it suggests music, celebration, or children's band instruments.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tambourine in music classes, church services, band contexts, and at parties. People say 'play the tambourine' or 'shake the tambourine' in casual speech. It is widely known and not formal.

distinctions.note: A timbrel is an ancient frame drum, often used in Bible translations, while a tambourine is the modern instrument with jingles.
A drum is struck with sticks or hands and has a membrane; a tambourine is shaken or struck and has metal jingles.

examples.everyday: My daughter got a tambourine for her birthday and now she shakes it all day.
examples.professional: The worship team needs a tambourine player for Sunday's service, so please let me know if you can help.
examples.analytical: In Psalm 150, the RSV's 'timbrel' is often read as a broader category of rhythmic percussion, which shows how ancient instruments are translated into modern terms.

nuance.analogy: A tambourine is like a drum that talks back with jingles every time you hit it.
nuance.etymology: From French tambourin, from Provençal tambori, meaning a small drum.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as 'tam-BOO-reen'.
Using 'tambourine' to mean any drum, when it specifically has jingles.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word behind the instrument is toph (תֹּף), often rendered as timbrel in the Revised Standard Version. In Exodus 15:20, Miriam the prophetess takes a timbrel in her hand and leads the women in celebration after the Red Sea crossing. Psalm 150:4 calls God's people to praise him with timbrel and dance, which shows the instrument's place in joyful worship.

senses.definition: Equivalent in meaning or effect; amounting to the same thing in practical terms, even if being technically distinct.

core.definition: Equal in effect or value to something else, even though it has a different name or form.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on the first syllable, TAN, with a lighter secondary stress on the final syllable. Many learners stress the last syllable or make the -ount sound like 'mount' with a long o, so keep it as 'mownt'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It is most often used to say that something amounts to a bad outcome, such as tantamount to admitting guilt.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tantamount in formal writing, news, legal and business settings, and serious debates. It is usually followed by 'to' and a noun: tantamount to a refusal. In casual conversation, people more often say 'basically the same as' or 'it's like saying', so tantamount can sound stiff if used in everyday chat.

distinctions.note: Equivalent is neutral and can be used for measurements or exchange rates; tantamount is used when one thing amounts to another in effect, often with a judgment.
Synonymous refers to words with the same meaning; tantamount refers to actions or situations that have the same effect.

examples.everyday: Skipping the rest of the meeting is basically tantamount to saying you don't care, so just show up.
examples.professional: Missing the security patch deadline is tantamount to leaving the system open to attack for another quarter.
examples.analytical: Refusing to define terms in the debate is tantamount to conceding the argument, because the opponent sets the criteria for victory.

nuance.analogy: Like a receipt that says 'cash' and a receipt that says 'card' but both show the same amount paid: different labels, the same result.
nuance.etymology: From Anglo-Norman tant amunter, 'to amount to as much', from Latin roots meaning 'so much' and 'to climb up'.
common_mistakes: Using tantamount with 'of' instead of 'to' (say tantamount to, not tantamount of).
Using it for simple equality of numbers; it is for effect or meaning, not math.
patterns: tantamount to sth (not before a noun)

senses.definition: Showing sympathy for small bad news.

core.definition: Said to show sympathy or mild disappointment when you hear small bad news.

pronunciation.tip: 'That's' is reduced to 'thats', 'too' is lightly stressed, and BAD gets the main stress. In fast speech, the words link together smoothly.

nuance.connotation: Polite and sympathetic, but light; it signals that the news is not serious.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in everyday situations, such as a store being out of an item or a friend missing an event. It is friendly and neutral, suitable for most settings. For more serious news, use 'I'm sorry to hear that' instead.

distinctions.note: Stronger, implying a harder experience; 'too bad' is for minor disappointments.
Similar in tone, but more often used for a missed chance or something you wish had gone differently.

examples.everyday: The store is out of oat milk? That's too bad.
examples.professional: The vendor can't deliver until next month? That's too bad, but we can adjust the schedule.
examples.analytical: Calling the failed experiment 'too bad' treats a methodological flaw as a minor setback rather than a lesson.

nuance.analogy: Like a small rain shower on a picnic day: disappointing, but nothing serious.
common_mistakes: Saying 'It is too bad' in speech; Americans usually say 'That's too bad.'
Using it for serious tragedies, which can sound dismissive.

conversation.text: "The restaurant was closed." "Oh, that's too bad."
That's too bad you can't make it tonight. Maybe next time.
"My flight got delayed." "That's too bad. How long?"

senses.definition: To issue someone a ticket, as for travel or for a violation of a local or traffic law.
To mark with a ticket.
senses.example: to ticket goods in a retail store

senses.definition: A service request, used to track complaints or requests that an issue be handled.
A small document that acts as proof of something, often thereby granting the holder some ability.
senses.example: I've got two tickets for the match on Saturday; want to come?

senses.definition: A pass entitling the holder to admission to a show, concert, sporting event, etc.
senses.example: I've got two tickets for the match on Saturday; want to come?

senses.definition: A pass entitling the holder to board a train, a bus, a plane, or other means of transportation.
senses.example: train ticket bus ticket plane ticket

senses.definition: A permit to operate a machine on a construction site.
A certificate or token of a share in a lottery or other scheme for distributing money, goods, etc.
senses.example: lottery ticket raffle ticket

senses.definition: A certificate of qualification as a ship's master, pilot, or other crew member.
A solution to a problem; something that is needed in order to do something.
senses.example: That's the ticket.

senses.definition: A citation for a traffic violation.
A list of candidates for an election, or a particular theme to a candidate's manifesto.
senses.example: Joe has joined the party's ticket for the county elections.

senses.definition: A label affixed to goods to show their price or description.
A warrant.
(dated) A small note or notice.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (dated) A tradesman's bill or account (hence the phrase on ticket and eventually on tick).
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (dated) A visiting card.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A printed slip proving you paid for a ride, show, or game, or a notice of a traffic fine.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable; the second syllable is a reduced 'it' with a short, unstressed vowel, not 'eet'. Don't stretch it into 'tick-EET'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can feel negative when it refers to a traffic or parking ticket.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'ticket' for travel tickets, event admission, and traffic or parking fines. Context tells you which: 'I got a ticket' on the highway almost always means a fine. For a flight, you show your boarding pass at the gate. A natural exchange is 'Did you get the tickets?' and 'Yep, they're on my phone.'

distinctions.note: A pass gives repeated or general access over a period, while a ticket usually grants one-time entry to one event or trip.
A receipt proves you bought something; a ticket usually grants access or a ride.

examples.everyday: I got a speeding ticket on the way home, so I'm not happy about it.
examples.professional: Please attach your ticket number when you email the airline about the refund.
examples.analytical: A ticket is a token of entitlement, and its value lies in the claim it gives the bearer rather than in the paper itself.

nuance.analogy: Like a permission slip you hand over at the door.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English 'ticket', from Old French 'estiquet', meaning a label or notice.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as a long 'eet', as in 'TIK-eet'.
Using 'ticket' for the money owed; Americans say 'pay the fine' and call the citation itself the ticket.

ticket.etymology: *tikkat*, *tikket*, from Middle French *etiquet*, *estiquet*, and *etiquette*, *estiquette* (“a bill, note, label, ticket”), from Old French *estechier* (“to attach, stick”), from **stikkjan*, **stekan* (“to stick, pierce, sting”), from Proto-Germanic…

conversation.text: I bought my train ticket on the app.
I got a ticket for parking in a loading zone.
I opened a ticket with IT about my laptop.

senses.definition: Introduces a statement you want no one to misunderstand.

core.definition: A phrase used to introduce a statement that you want no one to misunderstand.

pronunciation.tip: Reduce 'to' and stress 'CLEAR' with a clear, rhotic 'r'. Keep 'be' very short in speech, so it sounds like 'bee' only in careful speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can sound direct or slightly firm, especially when someone is setting a boundary.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use to be clear in meetings, emails, and arguments to make a point unmistakable, often before a decision or boundary. It can sound firm or even impatient if overused. A natural reply is 'Got it' or 'Okay, thanks for clarifying.'

distinctions.note: To be fair introduces a point that acknowledges the other side, while to be clear introduces a point you want understood without doubt.
In other words restates a point in simpler terms, while to be clear emphasizes that the statement is precise and not open to misreading.

examples.everyday: To be clear, I'm not upset, I just want to know when dinner will be ready.
examples.professional: To be clear, the release is approved, but we can't ship it until security signs off.
examples.analytical: To be clear, the author does not claim that all moral intuitions are reliable, only that some are more trustworthy than others.

nuance.analogy: To be clear is like turning on a bright light in a room so that nothing hides in the corner.
common_mistakes: Using to be clear to mean 'to be transparent' in physical description, where it is less natural.
Dropping 'be', as in 'to clear', which changes the meaning.

conversation.text: To be clear, nobody is losing their job.
I'm fine with the plan, to be clear. I just have one concern.
To be clear, we need the data by Wednesday at the latest.

senses.definition: Capable of being borne, tolerated or endured; bearable or endurable.
Moderate in degree; mediocre; passable, acceptable or so-so.
Such as to be tolerated or countenanced; permissible; allowable.
In fair health; passably well.

core.definition: Good enough to put up with; bearable, or acceptable but not especially good.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the 'ah' vowel as in 'cot', since most Americans merge this vowel with 'caught'. The final -able ends in a syllabic l, so don't add an extra vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It describes something acceptable but not pleasant or excellent.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say tolerable for weather, food or a job that is okay but not great. It sounds lukewarm, so it is a polite way to avoid complaining. People often say 'It's not bad' or 'It's fine' in a more positive tone. The formal sense of 'permissible' is less common in speech.

distinctions.note: Bearable focuses on pain or discomfort that you can endure, while tolerable can also describe food, weather or performance that is only passable.
Acceptable is a positive judgment that something meets a standard, while tolerable suggests it only just meets the standard.
Passable is more informal and often describes a skill or quality as just adequate, while tolerable can be used more widely.

examples.everyday: The coffee at the diner was tolerable, but I wouldn't go out of my way for it.
examples.professional: A two-second delay is tolerable for this dashboard, but anything longer will frustrate users.
examples.analytical: A theory that merely makes suffering tolerable has not yet shown that the suffering is justified.

nuance.analogy: Like a lukewarm shower that you can stand but would not choose.
nuance.etymology: From Latin tolerabilis, from tolerare, to bear or endure.
common_mistakes: Confusing tolerable with tolerant, which describes a person's attitude.
Using tolerable as strong praise, when it actually signals only moderate satisfaction.

tolerable.etymology: Middle English *tolerable*, borrowed from Middle French *tolerable*, from Latin *tolerābilis*.

senses.definition: To relax; to make quieter or less obtrusive; to make milder.
senses.example: Ask them to tone down that orange and pink color scheme a bit.

senses.definition: To make a television program, piece of writing, etc. less offensive and so more suitable for a family audience.
To moderate or relax; to diminish or weaken the striking characteristics of; to soften.

core.definition: To make something less intense, loud, extreme, or offensive, such as music, language, colors, or behavior.

pronunciation.tip: Stress DOWN most strongly. In fast speech the d of 'down' often blends into the n of 'tone', so it sounds close to 'tohn-DOWN'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, depending on context. It can suggest politeness or caution, but it can also imply that someone is being told to hold back.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'tone down' in everyday requests, such as asking someone to lower the volume or soften their words. The pronoun goes between 'tone' and 'down', as in 'tone it down'. A common natural reply is 'Sorry, I'll tone it down' or 'Okay, I'll be more calm'.

distinctions.note: Soften is broader and can refer to feelings or surfaces, while tone down is specifically about reducing intensity in behavior, sound, or language.
Calm down is about a person's emotions, while tone down is about the intensity of speech, music, or actions.

examples.everyday: Could you tone down the music a little? I'm trying to sleep.
examples.professional: Let's tone down the language in the email so it doesn't sound like we're blaming the vendor.
examples.analytical: The author toned down his critique of the church in later editions, perhaps to reach a wider audience.

nuance.analogy: Toning down is like turning a dimmer switch: you reduce the brightness without turning the light off.
nuance.etymology: Tone is from Greek tonos; down is from Old English dūn, 'downward'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'tone down it' instead of 'tone it down'.
Stressing 'tone' instead of 'down' in normal speech.

conversation.text: You might want to tone down your language in front of the kids.
The designer toned the colors down a bit.

senses.definition: Relating to a particular topic or subject.
senses.example: The book is divided into topical chapters.

senses.definition: Relating to a topic or subject of current interest.
senses.example: Fair trade has become quite a topical issue.

senses.definition: Local to a particular place.
Arranged according to topic or theme; thematic.
Applied to a localized part of the body.
Applied externally (to the surface of the skin or eye).
A substance, especially a medication, applied externally (to the surface of the skin or eye).
A topical anaesthetic.
A joke dealing with current events or topical subjects.
A postage stamp depicting a particular theme or subject (such as birds or trains), potentially sought out by topical stamp collectors.

core.definition: Relating to a current subject of public interest, or applied to the outside surface of the body, such as skin.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, TAH, and make the middle vowel a quick, reduced sound. The final syllable is a weak, reduced syllable and is often pronounced like 'kul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In medicine it is a technical term, and in conversation it describes something in the news.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use topical in two main ways: for current events in conversation or media ('a topical issue'), and in medicine for a cream or ointment applied to the skin. In everyday talk, 'current' or 'in the news' is often more natural.

distinctions.note: Topic is the noun for the subject itself, while topical describes something related to a current subject.
Local means nearby or within a region, while topical in medicine means applied to the outside surface of the body.

examples.everyday: That joke was pretty topical, since everyone at the office has been talking about the election.
examples.professional: The meeting agenda covered several topical issues, including the new data privacy rules.
examples.analytical: A topical debate can illuminate a deeper philosophical question, but it can also distract from the enduring principle beneath it.

nuance.analogy: Like a headline that is on everyone's mind this week.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin topicus, from Greek topikos, relating to topics or commonplaces.
common_mistakes: Confusing topical with topic, which is the noun.
Pronouncing the middle syllable as a full vowel, which sounds like 'TAH-pee-kal'.

senses.definition: Rail transport.
Elongated or trailing portion.
senses.example: Unfortunately, the leading bridesmaid stepped on the bride's train as they were walking down the aisle.

senses.definition: The elongated back portion of a dress or skirt (or an ornamental piece of material added to similar effect), which drags along the ground.
senses.example: Unfortunately, the leading bridesmaid stepped on the bride's train as they were walking down the aisle.

senses.definition: A trail or line of something, especially gunpowder.
The tail of a bird.
Connected sequence of people or things.
senses.example: Our party formed a train at the funeral parlor before departing for the burial.

senses.definition: A group of people following an important figure such as a king or noble; a retinue, a group of retainers.
A group of animals, vehicles, or people that follow one another in a line, such as a wagon train; a caravan or procession.
senses.example: Our party formed a train at the funeral parlor before departing for the burial.

senses.definition: A sequence of events or ideas which are interconnected; a course or procedure of something.
A set of things, events, or circumstances that follow after or as a consequence; aftermath, wake.
A set of interconnected mechanical parts which operate each other in sequence.
A series of electrical pulses.
A series of specified vehicles (originally tramcars in a mine as usual, later especially railway carriages) coupled together.

A mechanical (originally steam-powered, now typically diesel or electrical) vehicle carrying a large number of passengers and freight along a designated track or path, typically on rails; a line of such vehicles and wagons considered overall as a mode of transport.
senses.example: on a train

senses.definition: A service on a railway line.
A long, heavy sleigh used in Canada for the transportation of merchandise, wood, etc.
A software release schedule.
An act wherein series of men line up and then penetrate a person, especially as a form of gang rape.
A specified topic, behavior, interest or inclination.
senses.example: She doesn't come around any more, cuz she had a kid. She's on the family train now.

senses.definition: A transient trail of glowing ions behind a large meteor as it falls through the atmosphere or accompanying a comet as it nears the sun; tail.
The men and vehicles following an army, which carry artillery and other equipment for battle or siege.
(poetic) The elongated body or form of something narrow and winding, such as the course of a river or the body of a snake.
senses.label: poetic

senses.definition: (rare) An animal's trail or track.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (poetic) A group or class of people.
senses.label: poetic

senses.definition: To teach and form (someone) by practice; to educate (someone).
senses.example: You can't train a pig to write poetry.

senses.definition: To practice an ability.
senses.example: She trained seven hours a day to prepare for the Olympics.

senses.definition: To feed data into an algorithm, usually based on a neural network, to create a machine learning model that can perform some task.
To improve one's fitness.
senses.example: I trained with weights all winter.

senses.definition: To proceed in sequence.
To move (a gun) laterally so that it points in a different direction.
senses.example: The assassin had trained his gun on the minister.

senses.definition: To encourage (a plant or branch) to grow in a particular direction or shape, usually by pruning and bending.
senses.example: The vine had been trained over the pergola.

senses.definition: To transport (something) by train.
To travel by train.
To trace (a lode or any mineral appearance) to its head.
To create a trainer (cheat patch) for; to apply cheats to (a game).

core.definition: A connected group of railroad cars pulled by a locomotive, used to carry passengers or freight along tracks.

pronunciation.tip: This word rhymes with 'rain' and 'brain', with a long a and a clear r. Do not add a y sound or turn the vowel into 'e'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday word for transportation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use train for passenger or freight rail service, and they often say 'the train' for a commuter or intercity service. For travel in a city, people usually say subway, metro or light rail depending on the system. In casual talk, people also say 'catch the train' or 'miss the train' for getting or missing a ride.

distinctions.note: A subway is an underground urban rail system, while a train can be intercity, commuter or freight.
Railroad refers to the tracks, company or system, while train refers to the vehicle or service.

examples.everyday: We can take the train downtown, so we don't have to pay for parking.
examples.professional: Freight trains moved most of our warehouse supplies to the Midwest last week, which reduced our truck costs.
examples.analytical: The train appears repeatedly in American literature as a symbol of modernity, speed and the changing landscape.

nuance.analogy: A train is like a family walking in a line, with each car following the one in front and all pulled by the engine.
nuance.etymology: From Old French trahiner, to pull or drag, from Latin trahere.
common_mistakes: Saying 'in the train' instead of 'on the train'.
Confusing train with trainer or training, which are different word forms with different meanings.

train.etymology: From Middle English *trayne* (“train”), from Old French *train* (“a delay, a drawing out”), from *traïner* (“to pull out, to draw”), from Vulgar Latin **traginō*, from **tragō*, from Latin *trahō* (“to pull, to draw”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European…

conversation.text: The train to Boston leaves at 8:15 from track 6.
I missed my train and had to wait an hour.
We're training the new guy this week, so it's been busy.
She's training for a marathon this fall.

senses.definition: Of, caused by, or causing trauma.
Produced by wounds, especially as opposed to disease or other process.
senses.example: traumatic tetanus; traumatic brain injury

senses.definition: (dated) Adapted to the cure of wounds; vulnerary.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (dated) Of or relating to wounds; applied to wounds.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (dated) A medicine for wounds; a vulnerary.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: Deeply distressing and emotionally damaging, causing lasting psychological harm or injury.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the middle syllable, MAT, and keep the first syllable's vowel open, as in 'raw'. The final -ic is a short 'ik', not 'eek'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes events or experiences that cause serious distress, sometimes used loosely for anything upsetting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use traumatic for serious events, such as accidents, losses, or violence, and in psychology when discussing lasting effects. In casual speech people sometimes overuse it, as in 'the test was traumatic', which can sound exaggerated. Note that the old medical sense of wound-related is rare in daily life.

distinctions.note: Upsetting is a mild, everyday word for something that distresses you; traumatic describes events with serious, lasting psychological impact.
Painful can describe physical pain or emotional hurt; traumatic implies a deeper, more lasting injury, often from a single shocking event.

examples.everyday: Losing our dog in the storm was really traumatic for the kids, so we talk about it a lot.
examples.professional: The outage was traumatic for the on-call team, so we're scheduling a blameless review and some time off.
examples.analytical: A traumatic event is one that overwhelms a person's capacity to integrate experience, which explains why its memory may return involuntarily.

nuance.analogy: Like a sudden fall that breaks something inside, leaving the injury even after the surface heals.
nuance.etymology: From Greek trauma, 'wound', via Late Latin traumaticus, 'relating to wounds'.
common_mistakes: Using traumatic for minor frustrations, which sounds exaggerated in American speech.
Stressing the first syllable, as in TRAW-matic, instead of the middle.
Confusing the adjective with the noun trauma, which is a different part of speech.

traumatic.etymology: From the Latin *traumaticus*, from the Ancient Greek *τραυματικός*, from *τραῦμα*.

senses.definition: A small wheel; a caster or pulley.
A small wheel of cheese.
Ellipsis of truckle bed.
To roll or move upon truckles, or casters; to trundle.
To sleep in a truckle bed.
To act in a submissive manner; to fawn, submit to a superior. [with to]

core.definition: To submit meekly or fawn over a more powerful person, usually with the phrase 'truckle to'.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, TRUCK. The final 'le' is a weak 'ul' sound, not a separate syllable with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it suggests servile or undignified behavior toward someone with power.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'truckle' in everyday speech; it appears mostly in literary, political, or journalistic writing. It is stronger and more pointed than 'defer', and it implies a loss of dignity. If you use it, the 'to' phrase is standard, as in 'truckle to the boss'.

distinctions.note: Defer is neutral or polite, showing respect for another's authority, while truckle implies fawning or lost dignity.
Kowtow is more common in everyday American speech and suggests excessive deference, but it is more colloquial than truckle.

examples.professional: The senior engineer refused to truckle to the executives and insisted on the technical review.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that many intellectuals truckle to political power in the hope of patronage, sacrificing candor for access.

nuance.analogy: To truckle is like a dog that rolls over at the sight of its master, abandoning its own stance to please.
nuance.etymology: From 'truckle', a small wheel or caster, from the image of a bed on casters that slides under a larger bed, suggesting subordination.
common_mistakes: Using 'truckle' alone without 'to' when a person is the object of submission.
Confusing it with 'truck' or 'trundle', which refer to moving something on wheels.

senses.definition: Not qualified: ineligible; unfit for a position or task.
senses.example: His lack of a high school diploma renders him unqualified for the job.

senses.definition: Not elaborated upon; undescribed; unrestricted.
senses.example: The right to free speech is well established as not being an unqualified right to violent incitement nor to free amplification.

senses.definition: Outright; thorough; utter; unhampered.
senses.example: an unqualified success

core.definition: Not having the training, skills, or legal permission needed for a job or task; also used to mean complete or total.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KWAH, the second syllable. The final -ified is pronounced fyd, with a long i, and the middle vowel is reduced to ih.

nuance.connotation: Negative when it means not fit for a job; positive or emphatic when it means total support, as in unqualified support.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it to say someone is not fit for a role, as in he is unqualified for the position, often in hiring or politics. It is also used for emphasis, as in unqualified success or unqualified love. A natural reply to praise might be Absolutely, no question.

distinctions.note: Underqualified means not qualified enough, usually for a specific role, while unqualified can mean not qualified at all.
Unconditional means with no conditions or limits; unqualified is similar but is more often used for praise or agreement.

examples.everyday: My uncle says the new tacos are an unqualified success.
examples.professional: The hiring manager said the applicant was unqualified for the senior role because he lacked experience with the stack.
examples.analytical: Her claim that data always reveals truth is unqualified, which is precisely what makes it philosophically vulnerable.

nuance.analogy: Like a key that does not fit the lock; it is not the right tool for this door.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus qualified, from Medieval Latin qualificare, to give a quality to.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with underqualified when describing someone who has some relevant skill.
Using it as a noun; it is an adjective, so say unqualified candidates, not unqualifieds.

senses.definition: Containing hexavalent uranium.

core.definition: Relating to the planet Uranus, or in older usage, relating to the heavens or to a heavenly, spiritual kind of love.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable. Start with a 'y' sound, and the final syllable is reduced to a weak 'un.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical in astronomy; literary when used for heavenly or idealized love.
nuance.usage_note: The dictionary sense about containing hexavalent uranium is rare and technical, and most Americans would say 'uranyl' or 'uranium compound' instead. In everyday speech it is almost never used. In astronomy, 'Uranian' describes the planet Uranus or its moons, and in older literature it can mean heavenly or spiritual. Do not confuse it with 'uranium,' which is the element.

distinctions.note: 'Uranium' is the chemical element; 'uranian' is an adjective relating to the planet Uranus or heavenly things.
'Uranyl' names the uranium ion or compounds containing it, which is the chemistry term closest to the dictionary sense.

examples.everyday: My kid is into space, and she keeps asking about the Uranian moons.
examples.professional: The mission team modeled the Uranian magnetic field before choosing the flyby trajectory.
examples.analytical: Plato's distinction between a Uranian and a Pandemic Venus contrasts heavenly love with ordinary desire.

nuance.analogy: Like a word that points you to a distant planet, just as 'lunar' points to the moon.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'Uranus,' the Greek personification of the heavens, with the adjective suffix '-ian.'
common_mistakes: Confusing 'uranian' with 'uranium,' the element.
Using 'uranian' for ordinary things on Earth.

senses.definition: To seize and hold or use (powers, an office, a coat of arms, a right or copyright, etc) from another, without right (usually by illegitimate means).
To take the place of someone or something else; to supplant.

core.definition: To take power, a position, or a right from someone else, usually without legitimate authority or permission.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable. Keep the vowel as a strong rhotic 'er' sound, and end with a clear /p/. Do not confuse it with 'usury.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies taking something that belongs to another, illegitimately.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'usurp' in news, political writing, history, and literature to describe seizing power or authority. In everyday speech they say 'take over' or 'take someone's place,' which is more casual. The word is strong and may sound dramatic in ordinary conversation.

distinctions.note: 'Seize' is a general word for taking something by force, while 'usurp' specifically implies taking a right or role that is not yours.
'Supplant' means to replace someone, often by trickery, while 'usurp' focuses on wrongful seizure of power or rights.

examples.everyday: My little brother tried to usurp my spot on the couch, but I wasn't giving it up.
examples.professional: The new manager tried to usurp the team lead's role by approving budgets without consulting her.
examples.analytical: A tyrant who usurps the authority of the law places himself above the community that gave the law its legitimacy.

nuance.analogy: Like someone sitting in your chair at the head of the table and insisting it was always theirs.
nuance.etymology: From Old French usurper, from Latin usurpare, 'to seize for use,' from usus 'use' and rapere 'to seize.'
common_mistakes: Confusing 'usurp' with 'usury,' the charging of excessive interest.
Using 'usurp' for ordinary taking, such as 'usurp the cookies'; it implies a serious wrongful seizure.

usurp.etymology: From Middle English *usurpen*, from Old French *usurper*, from Latin *ūsūrpō*.

senses.definition: The state of being valid, authentic or genuine.
State of having legal force.
A quality of a measurement indicating the degree to which the measure reflects the underlying construct, that is, whether it measures what it purports to measure (see reliability).
The genuinity, as distinguished from the efficacity or the regularity, of a sacrament as a result of some formal dispositions being fulfilled.

core.definition: The quality of being logically sound, legally binding, or accurate; in research, whether a test measures what it is meant to measure.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LID, the second syllable. The first and last syllables are reduced, and the middle 't' is often a quick flap in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term that carries no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'validity' in academic writing, science, law, and statistics. In everyday speech they more often say 'whether something is valid' or 'whether it holds up'. In a professional setting, 'validity' often appears in research design or survey development.

distinctions.note: Reliability is consistency: a measure gives similar results repeatedly. Validity is accuracy: it measures what it is supposed to measure.
'Validity' is the quality or property. 'Validation' is the process of checking that quality.

examples.everyday: I'm not sure about the validity of that rumor, so let's check the news before we share it.
examples.professional: The team questioned the validity of the survey because the questions were worded in a leading way.
examples.analytical: The validity of a syllogism depends on its logical form, not on whether its premises happen to be true.

nuance.analogy: Validity is like a thermometer that reads the actual temperature rather than just giving the same wrong number every time.
nuance.etymology: From Latin validitas 'strength', from validus 'strong'.
common_mistakes: Confusing validity with reliability; a measure can be consistent but still measure the wrong thing.
Using 'validity' to mean 'truth' in logic; a valid argument can have a false premise.

validity.etymology: From *valid* + *ity*, borrowed from Middle French *validité*, from Late Latin *validitas*.

senses.definition: To speak boastfully.
To speak boastfully about.
To boast of; to make a vain display of; to display with ostentation.
An instance of vaunting; a boast.

core.definition: To boast about something, often in a showy way that draws attention to oneself and one's achievements.

pronunciation.tip: Use an open vowel like the one in 'taunt' or 'thought'; in General American the cot-caught merger means 'vawnt' and 'vahnt' are both acceptable. Pronounce the final t clearly.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests showy, unpleasant bragging, and it is used with a slight tone of disapproval.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'vaunt' in casual speech; they say 'brag' or 'show off' instead. You will mostly see it in newspaper essays, literary writing, and formal speeches. A natural reply to someone who vaunts their success is to change the subject or give a neutral remark.

distinctions.note: 'Brag' is informal and everyday; 'vaunt' is more formal and sounds more literary.
'Boast' can be neutral or mildly positive, as in 'the city boasts a great museum'; 'vaunt' is almost always negative.
'Flaunt' means to display something proudly to be admired, especially a possession; 'vaunt' means to boast in words.

examples.everyday: My neighbor keeps vaunting his new truck every time we talk over the fence.
examples.professional: She never vaunted her results in the meeting; she just showed the data and let it speak.
examples.analytical: Pride that vaunts its achievements has already forgotten how much of them it owed to others.

nuance.analogy: Vaunting is like holding up a trophy and reading out loud the names of everyone you beat.
nuance.etymology: From Old French 'vanter', from Latin 'vanitare', to boast, related to 'vanus', empty or vain.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'vaunt' with 'vain', which means conceited or futile, and is a different word.
Using 'vaunt' in casual conversation, where 'brag' or 'show off' sounds more natural.

vaunt.etymology: From Middle English *vaunten*, from Anglo-Norman *vaunter*, variant of Old French *vanter*, from Latin *vānus* (“vain, boastful”).

senses.definition: The quality of speaking or stating the truth; truthfulness.
Something that is true; a truthful statement; a truth.
Agreement with the facts; accordance with the truth; accuracy or precision.
Act of being exact and accurate.
Correctness and carefulness in one's plan of action.

core.definition: The quality of always telling the truth, or the accuracy of a statement or report.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on RAS, the second syllable. The final vowel is a weak 'ee' sound, and the flapped t in 'tee' sounds like a soft d in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes honesty or accuracy and is used respectfully.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use veracity mostly in formal, journalistic, legal, and academic contexts, such as questioning the veracity of a claim. In everyday speech they would more often say 'is it true' or 'accuracy'. Used about a person, it sounds serious and a little formal.

distinctions.note: Accuracy is about how closely something matches a standard or measurement. Veracity emphasizes truthfulness, especially in what is said or reported.
Truth is the general concept or a fact. Veracity is the quality of being truthful, or the reliability of a statement.
Honesty is a common personal virtue. Veracity is more formal and focuses on the truth of statements.

examples.everyday: I doubt the veracity of that story about the new restaurant, so let's check the reviews first.
examples.professional: Before we publish the dashboard, we need to verify the veracity of the survey data.
examples.analytical: The philosopher argues that the veracity of a belief depends on its correspondence with the facts.

nuance.analogy: Veracity is like a measuring tape that reads true: you can rely on what it tells you.
nuance.etymology: From Latin veracitas, from verax 'truthful'.
common_mistakes: Using 'veracity' as a verb, as in 'to veracity a claim'; the verb is 'verify'.
Pronouncing the middle syllable too strongly; the second syllable is weak.

veracity.etymology: From Middle French *véracité*, from Old French *veracitie*, from Medieval Latin *vērācitās* (“truthfulness”) (whence *-acity*), from Latin *vērāx* (“truthful, speaking truth”), from *vērus* (“true, real”).

senses.definition: The property of being viable; the ability to live or to succeed.

core.definition: The ability of a plan, business, product, or living thing to survive and succeed over time, or to work in practice.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on BIL, the third syllable, while the first syllable 'vye' is a long 'eye' sound. Do not stress the first syllable. The -ity ending is weak, like 'ih-tee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise analytical word, neither positive nor negative by itself.
nuance.usage_note: In American business and technical settings people use viability to ask whether a plan can actually work: 'financial viability' or 'long-term viability'. In casual conversation you would say 'Can this actually work?' or 'Will this survive?' It sounds formal, so use it in meetings, reports, and professional writing.

distinctions.note: Feasibility asks whether something can be done with available resources; viability asks whether it can survive and succeed over time.
Practicality describes how usable something is in daily life; viability is a broader judgment about survival and long-term success.

examples.everyday: I'm worried about the viability of the bakery with these rent increases.
examples.professional: Before we approve the budget, we need a viability assessment for the new product line.
examples.analytical: Philosophers ask whether a theory's viability depends on its predictive success or on its internal coherence.

nuance.analogy: Like a seed that can sprout and grow in real soil: the question is whether it can survive once it leaves the packet.
nuance.etymology: From viable plus -ity; viable comes from French vivable, from vivre, to live, from Latin vivere.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in VYE-uh-bil-i-tee, instead of stressing BIL.
Using viability for a single choice; say 'viable option', not 'viability option'.

senses.definition: The position from which something is observed or considered.
senses.example: From the top of the hill you get a good viewpoint of the town.

senses.definition: An angle, outlook or point of view.
senses.example: It is my personal viewpoint that veganism should be not only accepted, but actively encouraged by those in power.

core.definition: A particular way of thinking about something, shaped by your position, experience or beliefs; an opinion or perspective.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, 'VYOO', and the final syllable is 'point' with a clear 't'. In American speech, 'view' is often 'vyoo' and sometimes 'vyoo' with a soft 'y'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It presents an opinion respectfully as a position from which someone sees a matter.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use viewpoint in meetings, debates and everyday talk to say that someone sees things differently: 'From my viewpoint, the schedule is too tight.' It is a polite way to disagree. Americans also say 'point of view' with the same meaning, and both are equally natural.

distinctions.note: They mean the same thing; 'point of view' is slightly more common in everyday speech, while 'viewpoint' sounds a little more formal.
An opinion is a judgment; a viewpoint is the position from which you form it.

examples.everyday: From my viewpoint, we should just leave earlier and skip the traffic.
examples.professional: I'd like to hear the engineering viewpoint before we commit to this timeline.
examples.analytical: A feminist viewpoint can illuminate the assumptions hidden in traditional accounts of labor.

nuance.analogy: A viewpoint is like a seat in a stadium: the same game looks different depending on where you sit.
nuance.etymology: From view plus point, 'a position from which one sees'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'in my viewpoint' instead of 'from my viewpoint'.
Confusing it with the physical sense of a scenic lookout; in everyday talk it usually means opinion.

conversation.text: Pull over at the next viewpoint; I want to take some pictures.
From the viewpoint, you can see the whole valley.
The trail ends at a viewpoint above the lake.

senses.definition: A witty remark; a bon mot; an epigram; a zinger.

core.definition: A short, clever, and polished remark that is witty and often memorable.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, WIT. The final '-ism' is reduced to a weak 'iz-um', so avoid pronouncing it as a full 'iz-m' or 'izz-ism'.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it praises a remark for being clever and polished, though it can be used neutrally for any witty line.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'witticism' in writing, speeches, and reviews to describe a clever line, often in a formal or literary tone. In casual conversation they more often say 'a good one-liner', 'a zinger', or 'that was clever'. It is a good word for describing a famous remark, but not for a quick joke with friends.

distinctions.note: A 'joke' is a story or funny set-up with a punchline, while a 'witticism' is a brief, clever remark that may not be a joke.
A 'pun' is wordplay on sounds or meanings, while 'witticism' is a broader term for any clever, polished remark.

examples.everyday: She made a witticism about the traffic that had the whole table laughing.
examples.professional: The keynote speaker opened with a witticism about our release schedule, which broke the tension in the room.
examples.analytical: Wilde's witticisms conceal serious moral claims beneath their surface brilliance.

nuance.analogy: A witticism is like a well-cut gem: small, polished, and valued for the sharp light it throws.
nuance.etymology: From witty, plus the suffix -ism, so 'a witty expression'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, or saying 'wit-ih-SIZ-um' with the stress in the middle.
Using 'witticism' for a long funny story, which should be called a joke or an anecdote.

witticism.etymology: From *witty* + *icism*; coined in the 1670s by John Dryden, by analogy to *criticism*.

senses.definition: Resembling a wraith; ghostly.

core.definition: Resembling a wraith; pale, faint and ghostly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, RAYTH. The -like ending is pronounced like the word like, with a long i sound, not a short i.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to eerie. It describes something faint, pale or spectral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use wraithlike in literary description, art criticism and creative writing about mist, shadows or faint figures. In everyday speech they would say ghostly or like a ghost. It is not a common conversational word.

distinctions.note: Ghostly is common and can describe any eerie quality; wraithlike specifically suggests a thin, insubstantial, faint figure.
Spectral is more formal and technical, used in physics and literature; wraithlike is more descriptive and atmospheric.

examples.everyday: The fog rolled over the lake and made the trees look wraithlike.
examples.professional: On the low-resolution scan, the tumor appeared as a faint, wraithlike shadow that needed a second look.
examples.analytical: Her poems treat memory as a wraithlike presence, neither wholly absent nor fully present in the living moment.

nuance.analogy: A wraithlike figure is like a sketch in pencil: present, faint, and not fully solid.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the -like ending as lik, short i.
Using wraithlike for ordinary ghost stories in casual speech, where ghostly is more natural.

senses.definition: You are familiar with the situation I am describing; used to establish common ground with the interlocutor.

core.definition: A phrase that says 'you already understand the situation I am describing,' used to create shared understanding without explaining everything.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on NOH and MEEN, and 'what I' is quick and reduced. Americans often run the words together, so 'you know what I mean' may sound like 'yuh NOH wuh-ti-MEEN'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to friendly. It sounds warm and collaborative, but it can seem vague if you use it instead of explaining a real point.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this in casual talk to invite agreement after describing something hard to put into words, such as a feeling or a frustrating experience. A natural reply is 'Yeah, totally' or 'Yeah, I know what you mean.' Avoid using it in academic or business writing, where you should state the point directly.

distinctions.note: 'I mean' often introduces a clarification; 'you know what I mean' assumes the listener already shares your experience.
'You know' is a shorter filler; this phrase is a full appeal for shared understanding.

collocations: you know what I mean, right
say you know what I mean
I think you know what I mean
you know what I mean? Yeah
you know what I mean, it's just

examples.everyday: The waiter was nice but kind of rushed, you know what I mean?
examples.professional: The dashboard is technically correct, but it feels off to the stakeholders, you know what I mean?
examples.analytical: Some arguments persuade us without quite explaining why, and you know what I mean when we feel that pull.

nuance.analogy: Like two people holding the same photo: you do not need to describe every detail once you both see it.
common_mistakes: Using it when the listener does not share your experience, which can sound presumptuous.
Expecting it to work as a complete explanation in formal settings.

conversation.text: I just need a break from work, you know what I mean?
It's not that I don't like him; he's just a lot, you know what I mean?
"You know what I mean?" "Totally. I feel the same way."

core.definition: In the Bible, the last king of Judah, appointed by Babylon, who rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar and was taken into exile after Jerusalem fell.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the third syllable, KYE. Keep the first two syllables short and reduced, and end with a weak 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: Negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this name in Bible study, history of ancient Israel and sermons. Its connotation in scripture is negative, since the king is seen as breaking his oath to Babylon. Outside religious settings, it is rarely mentioned.

distinctions.note: Zedekiah was a king of Judah in the sixth century BC, while Zechariah is a prophet or priest name, so the two are never confused in context.

examples.everyday: In the history class we studied King Zedekiah and the fall of Jerusalem.
examples.professional: The timeline slide lists Zedekiah as the last king before the destruction of the temple.
examples.analytical: Jeremiah 37 to 39 depicts Zedekiah as weak and divided, unable to resist the pressure of his officials and of Babylon.

nuance.etymology: From the Hebrew tsidqiyyahu, meaning 'Yahweh is my righteousness'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in zed-ih-KY-uh.
Confusing Zedekiah with Zechariah.
nuance.biblical_note: Zedekiah (Hebrew tsidqiyyahu, 'Yahweh is my righteousness') was the last king of Judah, who reigned about 597 to 586 BC. Jeremiah 37 to 38 shows him consulting the prophet while Jerusalem was under siege. 2 Kings 25:7 says Zedekiah was blinded after he was captured and taken to Babylon. The name also belongs to a false prophet in 1 Kings 22:11, who opposed Micaiah.

core.definition: A town in southern Judah given to David by the Philistine king Achish, where David lived while in Philistine service and which was later raided by Amalekites.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and keep the 'i' short as in 'sick.' Pronounce the final 'g' as a hard sound, as in 'bag.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Ziklag is a place name used in Bible study, sermons and historical discussions of David. Americans may say it in church or when talking about the Bible, but it is not used in everyday speech. It is a standard name in English Bibles, including the RSV.

examples.everyday: When we read about David in 1 Samuel, my friend asked where Ziklag was, and I told him it was a town David was given by the Philistines.
examples.professional: In my lesson on David's wilderness years, I use Ziklag to show how he was caught between Philistine service and loyalty to Israel.
examples.analytical: The narrative of Ziklag's burning in 1 Samuel 30 serves as a turning point that reveals David's reliance on God through a priest's oracle.

nuance.analogy: Ziklag is like a temporary base camp: a place that was given, lived in and then lost and recovered, marking the stages of a journey.
common_mistakes: Confusing Ziklag with Zion or Zin, which are different places.
Placing the stress on the second syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: Ziklag was a town in the southern part of Judah, later assigned to the tribe of Simeon. The key passages are 1 Samuel 27:6, where Achish gives Ziklag to David and it becomes a royal possession of Judah; 1 Samuel 30:1-3, where Amalekites raid and burn the town while David's men are away and carry off their families; and Joshua 19:5, which lists Ziklag among the Simeonite towns. Nehemiah 11:28 also mentions it among towns resettled after the exile.
